units.title: Cardiac output
units.mechanism: Cardiac output equals heart rate multiplied by stroke volume. Stroke volume is EDV minus ESV, so changes in filling or emptying can change output even if heart rate is unchanged.
units.case: A patient has a heart rate of 75/min, EDV of 120 mL, and ESV of 50 mL. The calculated flow from the left ventricle is 5.25 L/min.
units.pitfall: A normal heart rate does not guarantee normal forward flow; stroke volume also matters.
units.objective: Explain cardiac output and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Mean arterial pressure
units.mechanism: At ordinary heart rates, MAP is approximately diastolic pressure plus one third of pulse pressure. More generally, MAP minus right atrial pressure equals cardiac output multiplied by systemic vascular resistance.
units.case: A blood pressure of 120/60 mmHg corresponds to an estimated average arterial driving pressure of 80 mmHg at a normal heart rate.
units.pitfall: The one-third approximation becomes less reliable at very high heart rates because the relative duration of diastole changes.
units.objective: Explain mean arterial pressure and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Frank–Starling mechanism
units.mechanism: Increased end-diastolic fiber length increases force generation within the physiologic range through length-dependent activation. This is movement along a given ventricular function curve rather than an increase in intrinsic contractility.
units.case: After a modest fluid bolus, stroke volume rises without a change in sympathetic stimulation or in the slope of the end-systolic pressure–volume relationship.
units.pitfall: More preload is not always beneficial: a failing ventricle may develop congestion with little increase in forward output.
units.objective: Explain frank–starling mechanism and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Preload
units.mechanism: Preload describes myocardial fiber stretch before contraction and is often approximated by end-diastolic volume. Filling pressure is only an indirect surrogate because compliance affects the pressure–volume relationship.
units.case: Two ventricles have the same end-diastolic volume but different filling pressures because one has a stiffer wall.
units.pitfall: A filling pressure should not be treated as interchangeable with ventricular volume when compliance differs.
units.objective: Explain preload and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Afterload
units.mechanism: Afterload is the load opposing ventricular ejection and relates to arterial pressure, outflow impedance, and wall stress. An acute increase at fixed preload and contractility increases ESV and decreases stroke volume.
units.case: An abrupt rise in aortic pressure makes the left ventricular pressure–volume loop taller and narrower on the next beat.
units.pitfall: SVR contributes to afterload but does not capture all of its components, including valve obstruction and arterial stiffness.
units.objective: Explain afterload and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Contractility
units.mechanism: Increased inotropy raises force generation at a given preload and afterload. It steepens the end-systolic pressure–volume relationship, reduces ESV, and increases stroke volume and ejection fraction.
units.case: A β1 agonist shifts the end-systolic pressure–volume relationship upward and to the left without requiring greater initial filling.
units.pitfall: Ejection fraction is load-dependent, so a change in EF alone does not isolate intrinsic contractility.
units.objective: Explain contractility and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Ventricular compliance
units.mechanism: Compliance is the change in volume divided by the corresponding change in pressure. A stiff ventricle requires higher diastolic pressure for a given volume, shifting the end-diastolic pressure–volume curve upward.
units.case: A patient has normal EF but elevated LV filling pressure and pulmonary congestion because the ventricle relaxes poorly and resists filling.
units.pitfall: Preserved EF does not exclude clinically important heart failure or impaired diastolic function.
units.objective: Explain ventricular compliance and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Pressure–volume loop phases
units.mechanism: Isovolumetric contraction begins after AV valve closure and precedes semilunar valve opening. Isovolumetric relaxation begins after semilunar closure; volume is unchanged while pressure falls because all valves are closed.
units.case: On a ventricular loop, pressure changes vertically while cavity volume stays fixed between valve closure and opening.
units.pitfall: A vertical segment is not an ejection phase: ejection requires an open outflow valve and falling ventricular volume.
units.objective: Explain pressure–volume loop phases and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Stroke work
units.mechanism: External ventricular stroke work is the area enclosed by the pressure–volume loop. It reflects pressure generation and volume ejected during a beat, whereas myocardial oxygen consumption also includes other energetic costs.
units.case: Two loops have the same stroke volume, but the one ejecting against a higher pressure encloses a larger area.
units.pitfall: Loop area represents mechanical work, not the entirety of myocardial energy use.
units.objective: Explain stroke work and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Ejection fraction
units.mechanism: EF equals stroke volume divided by EDV. For EDV 140 mL and ESV 84 mL, SV is 56 mL and EF is 40 percent; the ratio describes fractional emptying, not total systemic perfusion.
units.case: A dilated ventricle ejects 56 mL from an initial volume of 140 mL, producing a fractional emptying of 0.40.
units.pitfall: A normal EF can coexist with low stroke volume when the end-diastolic cavity is small.
units.objective: Explain ejection fraction and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Coronary perfusion timing
units.mechanism: Left ventricular contraction compresses intramyocardial vessels, limiting left coronary flow during systole. Most LV perfusion occurs during diastole, with driving pressure approximated by aortic diastolic pressure minus LV end-diastolic pressure.
units.case: Tachycardia and elevated LV filling pressure reduce the time and pressure gradient available to perfuse the left ventricular subendocardium.
units.pitfall: The right ventricle has lower systolic pressure, so right coronary flow is less restricted to diastole.
units.objective: Explain coronary perfusion timing and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Myocardial oxygen demand
units.mechanism: Heart rate, contractility, and ventricular wall stress are major determinants of myocardial oxygen demand. The myocardium already extracts a high fraction of arterial oxygen at rest, so increased demand is met mainly by increased coronary flow.
units.case: Exercise raises cardiac metabolic requirements, requiring coronary vasodilation rather than a large increase in already-high resting oxygen extraction.
units.pitfall: Do not infer adequate oxygen delivery from a normal coronary lumen alone; anemia, tachycardia, or low perfusion pressure can still matter.
units.objective: Explain myocardial oxygen demand and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Laplace wall stress
units.mechanism: Ventricular wall stress rises with intracavitary pressure and chamber radius and falls with wall thickness. Pressure overload encourages concentric thickening that initially reduces stress, whereas dilation increases the mechanical burden.
units.case: A dilated thin-walled ventricle must generate more wall tension than a smaller thick-walled ventricle at the same internal pressure.
units.pitfall: Simple geometric formulas approximate the ventricle and should be used to reason about direction, not exact patient-specific stress.
units.objective: Explain laplace wall stress and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Venous return
units.mechanism: Venous return is driven by the difference between mean systemic filling pressure and right atrial pressure, divided by resistance to venous return. At steady state, venous return and cardiac output are equal.
units.case: Increased venous tone recruits unstressed blood volume, raises mean systemic filling pressure, and increases the pressure gradient returning blood to the heart.
units.pitfall: High right atrial pressure can impede venous return rather than indicating that more blood is effectively reaching the left ventricle.
units.objective: Explain venous return and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Poiseuille resistance
units.mechanism: For ideal laminar flow, resistance is proportional to viscosity and tube length and inversely proportional to the fourth power of radius. Small changes in arteriolar radius therefore have large effects on flow resistance.
units.case: In an ideal vessel, halving the radius while holding length and viscosity constant increases resistance sixteenfold.
units.pitfall: The relationship is a physiologic approximation; real vessels are compliant and blood flow can be pulsatile or turbulent.
units.objective: Explain poiseuille resistance and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Fick cardiac output
units.mechanism: The Fick principle calculates cardiac output as oxygen consumption divided by the arterial–mixed venous oxygen content difference. Oxygen contents must use matching units; a denominator expressed per deciliter requires conversion to liters.
units.case: Oxygen consumption is 250 mL/min and the arterial–mixed venous oxygen difference is 50 mL/L. Estimated systemic flow is 5 L/min.
units.pitfall: Partial pressure is not interchangeable with oxygen content in the denominator of the Fick equation.
units.objective: Explain fick cardiac output and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Oxygen content
units.mechanism: Arterial oxygen content is approximately 1.34 times hemoglobin times fractional saturation plus 0.003 times PaO2, in mL O2/dL. Hemoglobin-bound oxygen accounts for most content under ordinary conditions.
units.case: A patient with severe anemia has a normal PaO2 and oxygen saturation but reduced oxygen carried per unit of blood.
units.pitfall: Normal saturation does not establish normal oxygen content when hemoglobin concentration is low.
units.objective: Explain oxygen content and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Baroreceptor reflex
units.mechanism: Carotid sinus and aortic arch stretch receptors signal through cranial nerves IX and X. Falling arterial pressure reduces firing, increases sympathetic output, and decreases vagal tone, raising heart rate and vascular tone.
units.case: On standing abruptly, reduced arterial stretch triggers tachycardia and arteriolar constriction within seconds.
units.pitfall: Baroreceptors respond rapidly but reset during sustained hypertension; they are not the sole controllers of long-term pressure.
units.objective: Explain baroreceptor reflex and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Dynamic exercise response
units.mechanism: During dynamic exercise, sympathetic drive increases heart rate and contractility while local metabolites dilate vessels in active muscle. Cardiac output rises and total systemic resistance usually falls; systolic pressure rises more than diastolic pressure.
units.case: A healthy runner develops increased cardiac output and systolic pressure with lower overall systemic resistance during sustained activity.
units.pitfall: Static resistance exercise can produce a different pressure response; do not generalize every exercise pattern to all activity.
units.objective: Explain dynamic exercise response and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Heart sound timing
units.mechanism: S1 occurs with closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves at the start of systole. S2 occurs with aortic and pulmonic closure at the end of systole; inspiration normally delays pulmonic closure and widens splitting.
units.case: Auscultation reveals a split second sound that becomes wider with inspiration and narrows on expiration in an otherwise healthy person.
units.pitfall: A fixed split or paradoxical split is different from normal respiratory variation and requires a different mechanism.
units.objective: Explain heart sound timing and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Ventricular phase 0
units.mechanism: Rapid depolarization in working ventricular myocytes is mediated by fast voltage-gated sodium channels. Sodium-channel blockade slows conduction in this tissue and can widen the QRS complex.
units.case: A drug slows the upstroke of the ventricular action potential and prolongs ventricular conduction on the surface ECG.
units.pitfall: Nodal tissue uses a calcium-dependent upstroke; the same phase number does not imply the same ion in every cell type.
units.objective: Explain ventricular phase 0 and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Ventricular plateau
units.mechanism: During phase 2, inward L-type calcium current balances outward potassium currents. The plateau supports calcium-induced calcium release and a prolonged refractory period that prevents tetanic contraction.
units.case: A ventricular myocyte maintains a prolonged near-zero membrane potential after its initial rapid depolarization while calcium enters the cell.
units.pitfall: A long cardiac action potential is functionally important because the heart must relax between contractions.
units.objective: Explain ventricular plateau and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Ventricular repolarization
units.mechanism: Phase 3 of the ventricular action potential is produced mainly by outward potassium currents as calcium current declines. Delayed repolarization lengthens the action potential and can increase the QT interval.
units.case: Blocking delayed rectifier potassium currents prolongs the return of ventricular membrane voltage toward its resting level.
units.pitfall: QT changes reflect more than one current and should be interpreted with heart rate and the clinical setting.
units.objective: Explain ventricular repolarization and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Nodal phase 0
units.mechanism: The upstroke in SA and AV nodal cells depends mainly on L-type calcium channels. Non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers slow AV nodal conduction and may prolong the PR interval.
units.case: Verapamil reduces the slope of depolarization in a cell located in the AV node rather than in ventricular muscle.
units.pitfall: Fast sodium channels dominate phase 0 in atrial and ventricular working myocytes, not in nodal pacemaker cells.
units.objective: Explain nodal phase 0 and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Funny current
units.mechanism: Hyperpolarization-activated HCN channels carry the mixed inward funny current contributing to spontaneous phase 4 depolarization. cAMP increases pacemaker activity; ivabradine reduces sinus rate by inhibiting this current.
units.case: A sinus-node drug lowers heart rate by reducing spontaneous diastolic depolarization without directly blocking ventricular fast sodium channels.
units.pitfall: The funny current is not the only contributor to phase 4, which also involves changing potassium and calcium currents.
units.objective: Explain funny current and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Beta-1 signaling
units.mechanism: β1 receptor stimulation activates Gs, adenylyl cyclase, cAMP, and protein kinase A. Increased calcium handling enhances contractility, while nodal effects increase pacemaker rate and AV conduction.
units.case: Sympathetic stimulation increases sinus rate, AV nodal conduction, and ventricular force through a cAMP-linked receptor.
units.pitfall: Atropine acts by removing muscarinic inhibition rather than directly stimulating β1 receptors.
units.objective: Explain beta-1 signaling and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Muscarinic M2 signaling
units.mechanism: Cardiac M2 receptors couple to Gi, reduce cAMP, and increase potassium conductance in nodal cells. Vagal stimulation slows SA discharge and AV conduction, with less direct effect on ventricular contractility.
units.case: A vagal maneuver slows AV nodal conduction by activating an inhibitory G-protein pathway and increasing nodal potassium conductance.
units.pitfall: Vagal maneuvers affect AV node-dependent rhythms differently from rhythms arising independently in ventricular tissue.
units.objective: Explain muscarinic m2 signaling and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: PR interval
units.mechanism: The PR interval extends from onset of atrial depolarization to onset of ventricular depolarization and includes AV nodal delay. A consistently prolonged interval above 200 ms with every P conducted indicates first-degree AV block.
units.case: Every P wave is followed by a QRS, but the interval from P onset to QRS onset is consistently 240 ms.
units.pitfall: A long PR is delayed conduction, not necessarily intermittent failure of impulses to reach the ventricles.
units.objective: Explain pr interval and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: QRS complex
units.mechanism: The QRS represents ventricular depolarization. Widening can result from bundle-branch block, ventricular origin of activation, sodium-channel blockade, or metabolic conduction disturbance such as severe hyperkalemia.
units.case: A rhythm originating in ventricular muscle spreads outside the normal rapid conduction system and produces broad complexes.
units.pitfall: A broad QRS does not identify a single cause by itself; rhythm context and associated findings matter.
units.objective: Explain qrs complex and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: QT interval
units.mechanism: The QT spans ventricular depolarization and repolarization and varies with heart rate. QT correction estimates rate-adjusted duration; prolonged repolarization predisposes to early afterdepolarizations and torsades de pointes.
units.case: A patient taking a repolarization-prolonging drug develops a long corrected QT and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia after a pause.
units.pitfall: Bazett correction can misestimate QT at extreme heart rates; a corrected number is not a substitute for clinical interpretation.
units.objective: Explain qt interval and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: First-degree AV block
units.mechanism: All atrial impulses conduct to the ventricles, but AV conduction is delayed, producing a prolonged constant PR interval. No QRS complexes are dropped because of block in this pattern.
units.case: A tracing has a regular rhythm with PR 220 ms and one QRS after every P wave, without progressive PR change or dropped beats.
units.pitfall: PR prolongation alone does not meet the definition of second-degree AV block.
units.objective: Explain first-degree av block and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Mobitz type I block
units.mechanism: Wenckebach block typically occurs in the AV node and shows progressive PR lengthening followed by a nonconducted P wave. The cycle then repeats, often with grouped beating.
units.case: Successive beats have longer PR intervals until a P wave is not followed by a QRS, after which conduction resumes with a shorter PR.
units.pitfall: Not every second-degree block is nodal; Mobitz type II has a different pattern and greater risk of progression.
units.objective: Explain mobitz type i block and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Mobitz type II block
units.mechanism: Intermittent atrial impulses fail to conduct despite a stable PR interval in conducted beats, often indicating His–Purkinje disease. The pattern can progress to complete AV block.
units.case: An ECG shows sudden dropped QRS complexes without preceding PR prolongation and a stable PR on the conducted beats.
units.pitfall: A 2:1 conduction pattern alone often cannot reliably distinguish Mobitz I from Mobitz II.
units.objective: Explain mobitz type ii block and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Third-degree AV block
units.mechanism: Complete interruption of atrial-to-ventricular conduction produces independent atrial and ventricular rhythms. An escape focus maintains ventricular activation, and the PR relationship varies without organized conduction.
units.case: P waves march through at one rate while QRS complexes occur at a slower independent rate with no fixed PR relationship.
units.pitfall: AV dissociation can have causes beyond complete block; the overall tracing must establish the conduction pattern.
units.objective: Explain third-degree av block and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Atrial fibrillation
units.mechanism: Disorganized atrial activation eliminates organized P waves and produces an irregularly irregular ventricular response when AV conduction is intact. Atrial stasis, especially in the left atrial appendage, increases thromboembolic risk.
units.case: An ECG shows no consistent P waves and unpredictable R–R intervals in a patient with an enlarged left atrium.
units.pitfall: An irregular rhythm is not automatically AF; multifocal atrial tachycardia and frequent ectopy can also be irregular.
units.objective: Explain atrial fibrillation and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Atrial flutter
units.mechanism: A macroreentrant atrial circuit produces organized rapid atrial activity, often with sawtooth flutter waves. AV conduction ratios such as 2:1 can generate a ventricular rate near 150/min when atrial rate is near 300/min.
units.case: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia near 150/min is accompanied by repetitive sawtooth atrial deflections, particularly in inferior leads.
units.pitfall: A ventricular rate near 150 is a clue, not proof; atrial activity and conduction relationships establish the diagnosis.
units.objective: Explain atrial flutter and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: AV nodal reentry
units.mechanism: Dual AV nodal pathways with differing conduction and refractory properties can sustain a reentrant loop. The resulting tachycardia is commonly regular and narrow, with atrial activation hidden in or immediately after the QRS.
units.case: A patient has abrupt onset and offset of a regular narrow-complex tachycardia that terminates when AV nodal conduction is transiently blocked.
units.pitfall: Not every supraventricular tachycardia is AV nodal reentry; accessory-pathway-mediated reentry can behave similarly.
units.objective: Explain av nodal reentry and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Wolff–Parkinson–White pattern
units.mechanism: An accessory AV pathway can bypass normal AV nodal delay, causing a short PR interval, delta wave, and widened QRS in sinus rhythm. It can also participate in reentrant tachycardia.
units.case: A baseline ECG shows a slurred initial QRS upstroke and short PR before episodes of rapid palpitations.
units.pitfall: AV nodal blockers can be dangerous in pre-excited atrial fibrillation because conduction through the accessory pathway may accelerate.
units.objective: Explain wolff–parkinson–white pattern and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Hyperkalemic ECG progression
units.mechanism: Rising extracellular potassium can produce peaked T waves, PR prolongation, P-wave loss, and QRS widening, potentially progressing to a sine-wave pattern. Severe hyperkalemia destabilizes conduction and requires urgent assessment.
units.case: A patient with renal failure develops tall peaked T waves followed by widening QRS complexes as potassium rises.
units.pitfall: ECG findings are variable and cannot reliably exclude dangerous hyperkalemia when absent.
units.objective: Explain hyperkalemic ecg progression and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Torsades de pointes
units.mechanism: This polymorphic ventricular tachycardia occurs in the setting of prolonged repolarization and often follows early afterdepolarizations. Drug effects, low potassium, low magnesium, and congenital long-QT syndromes are important settings.
units.case: After starting a QT-prolonging drug, a patient develops pause-associated polymorphic VT with complexes appearing to twist around the baseline.
units.pitfall: Polymorphic VT with a normal QT may have another mechanism, including acute ischemia.
units.objective: Explain torsades de pointes and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Stable angina
units.mechanism: A fixed coronary atherosclerotic narrowing limits flow reserve, creating demand-induced ischemia without acute myocardial necrosis. Symptoms are reproducible with exertion and improve when demand falls.
units.case: A patient develops predictable substernal pressure while climbing stairs that resolves after several minutes of rest, without evidence of acute myocardial injury.
units.pitfall: Relief with nitroglycerin is not specific enough to diagnose coronary ischemia on its own.
units.objective: Explain stable angina and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Plaque rupture
units.mechanism: Disruption of a vulnerable fibrous cap exposes thrombogenic material and activates platelets and coagulation. Acute thrombus formation can rapidly reduce coronary perfusion even when the preexisting narrowing was not severe.
units.case: A previously noncritical coronary plaque with a thin fibrous cap develops surface disruption and an acute superimposed thrombus.
units.pitfall: Plaque instability, not just percent stenosis, contributes to acute coronary syndromes.
units.objective: Explain plaque rupture and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Unstable angina
units.mechanism: New, worsening, or rest ischemic symptoms can occur without a diagnostic rise and fall of cardiac troponin indicating acute myocardial necrosis. Plaque disruption and incomplete thrombosis are common mechanisms.
units.case: A patient has new episodes of chest pressure at rest, ischemic ECG changes, and serial troponin values that do not establish myocardial injury.
units.pitfall: High-sensitivity assays reclassify many formerly labeled cases; serial testing and clinical context are essential.
units.objective: Explain unstable angina and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: NSTEMI
units.mechanism: Acute myocardial infarction requires a rise or fall in troponin with evidence of ischemia. When persistent diagnostic ST elevation is absent, the syndrome is classified as NSTEMI; subendocardial injury is a common pattern.
units.case: A patient has ischemic chest pain, ST depression, and a rise and fall in cardiac troponin without persistent ST elevation.
units.pitfall: An elevated troponin alone establishes myocardial injury, not necessarily an ischemic infarction.
units.objective: Explain nstemi and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: STEMI
units.mechanism: Acute persistent coronary occlusion can cause regional transmural ischemia and characteristic ST elevation in contiguous leads. Prompt recognition is critical because ongoing ischemia progressively destroys myocardium.
units.case: Severe ongoing chest pain is accompanied by new ST elevation in a coronary distribution and reciprocal changes in opposing leads.
units.pitfall: ST elevation also occurs in pericarditis, early repolarization, and other conditions; the pattern and context matter.
units.objective: Explain stemi and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: LAD territory
units.mechanism: The left anterior descending artery usually supplies the anterior LV wall, anterior interventricular septum, and apex. Occlusion commonly produces anterior precordial ischemic changes.
units.case: An infarct affects the anterior ventricular wall and anterior septum with ST elevation in leads V1–V4.
units.pitfall: Coronary anatomy varies, so lead localization is an anatomic guide rather than a perfect map.
units.objective: Explain lad territory and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: RCA inferior territory
units.mechanism: In right-dominant circulation, the RCA gives rise to the posterior descending artery and often supplies the inferior wall and AV node. Inferior infarction can therefore coexist with bradycardia or AV block.
units.case: A patient has ST elevation in II, III, and aVF with new AV nodal conduction delay in a right-dominant coronary system.
units.pitfall: The circumflex can supply the inferior territory in left-dominant circulation.
units.objective: Explain rca inferior territory and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Circumflex lateral territory
units.mechanism: The left circumflex artery supplies portions of the lateral LV through obtuse marginal branches. Ischemia can affect lateral leads such as I, aVL, V5, and V6 depending on branch anatomy.
units.case: A coronary lesion compromises the lateral LV wall supplied by obtuse marginal branches.
units.pitfall: Lateral wall changes may also involve diagonal branches of the LAD; territory localization is not perfectly exclusive.
units.objective: Explain circumflex lateral territory and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Coronary dominance
units.mechanism: Dominance is defined by the artery that gives rise to the posterior descending artery, rather than by the artery with the largest lumen or total flow. Right dominance is most common.
units.case: Angiography shows the posterior descending artery arising from the left circumflex, identifying a left-dominant system.
units.pitfall: Dominance does not mean that one artery supplies the entire heart.
units.objective: Explain coronary dominance and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Troponin interpretation
units.mechanism: Cardiac troponin indicates myocardial cell injury. A dynamic change plus evidence of ischemia supports infarction; sepsis, myocarditis, tachyarrhythmia, pulmonary embolism, and other processes can also elevate it.
units.case: A patient with viral myocarditis has a raised cardiac troponin without evidence that a coronary thrombus caused the injury.
units.pitfall: Do not equate every abnormal troponin with type 1 myocardial infarction.
units.objective: Explain troponin interpretation and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: CK-MB and reinfarction
units.mechanism: CK-MB usually returns toward baseline sooner than troponin after infarction, historically making a new rise useful when reinfarction is suspected. Modern assessment also relies on serial troponin changes and clinical evidence.
units.case: A patient develops recurrent ischemic pain several days after an MI and has a renewed rise in a marker that had already fallen toward baseline.
units.pitfall: Biomarker timing varies; a diagnosis of reinfarction cannot rest on an isolated laboratory number.
units.objective: Explain ck-mb and reinfarction and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Early infarct histology
units.mechanism: Coagulative necrosis evolves during the first day after ischemic cell death, with hypereosinophilic myocytes and loss of nuclei. Neutrophils accumulate over the following early days as acute inflammation develops.
units.case: Histology within the first few days of an infarct shows necrotic cardiac fibers and prominent neutrophilic infiltration.
units.pitfall: Very early infarction may have little visible light-microscopic change, and exact timelines overlap.
units.objective: Explain early infarct histology and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Macrophage clearance
units.mechanism: Around days 3–7 after infarction, macrophages clear dead myocardium before strong collagen replacement is established. The mechanically weakened tissue is vulnerable to rupture.
units.case: Several days after an MI, tissue sections show extensive phagocytosis of dead fibers with little mature collagen support.
units.pitfall: This vulnerable interval is approximate and can be altered by reperfusion and infarct size.
units.objective: Explain macrophage clearance and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Free-wall rupture
units.mechanism: Infarcted ventricular free wall can tear during tissue breakdown, allowing blood into the pericardial space. Hemopericardium can rapidly produce tamponade and hemodynamic collapse.
units.case: Five days after a large MI, a patient suddenly collapses with elevated JVP and blood accumulating around the heart.
units.pitfall: Papillary muscle rupture produces acute regurgitation rather than blood entering the pericardial sac.
units.objective: Explain free-wall rupture and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Septal rupture
units.mechanism: Postinfarction rupture of the interventricular septum creates an acute left-to-right shunt. A new harsh holosystolic murmur, shock, and a right ventricular oxygen saturation step-up are important clues.
units.case: Several days after an MI, a new loud murmur develops with a sudden increase in oxygen saturation between the right atrium and right ventricle.
units.pitfall: A new post-MI systolic murmur can also indicate papillary muscle rupture; the shunt finding distinguishes septal disruption.
units.objective: Explain septal rupture and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Papillary muscle rupture
units.mechanism: Ischemic rupture of a papillary muscle causes acute severe mitral regurgitation, pulmonary edema, and possible shock. The posteromedial muscle is vulnerable because it typically has a single arterial supply through the PDA.
units.case: After an inferior MI, sudden pulmonary edema and a new apical systolic murmur appear without a ventricular oxygen saturation step-up.
units.pitfall: Acute severe MR can have a relatively soft murmur when left ventricular and atrial pressures equalize rapidly.
units.objective: Explain papillary muscle rupture and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: True ventricular aneurysm
units.mechanism: A healed transmural infarct can form a broad-based dyskinetic outpouching containing scarred ventricular wall. It can cause mural thrombus, arrhythmia, and persistent ST elevation but is less rupture-prone than a pseudoaneurysm.
units.case: Weeks after a large anterior MI, imaging shows a broad-necked outpouching made of scarred myocardium with mural thrombus.
units.pitfall: A contained free-wall rupture is a pseudoaneurysm and carries a different rupture risk.
units.objective: Explain true ventricular aneurysm and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Dressler syndrome
units.mechanism: Delayed autoimmune inflammation of the pericardium can follow myocardial injury. Pleuritic positional pain, fever, and a friction rub may develop weeks after infarction.
units.case: Several weeks after an MI, a patient develops fever and chest pain relieved by leaning forward with a new friction rub.
units.pitfall: Early postinfarction pericarditis arises directly over injured myocardium and has a different timing from the delayed immune syndrome.
units.objective: Explain dressler syndrome and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Vasospastic angina
units.mechanism: Transient coronary smooth-muscle constriction can produce ischemia and episodic ST elevation, often at rest. The mechanism differs from fixed demand-limiting atherosclerotic stenosis.
units.case: A patient has recurrent early-morning chest pain at rest with transient ST elevation that resolves when coronary spasm relaxes.
units.pitfall: A normal angiogram between episodes does not exclude dynamic coronary spasm.
units.objective: Explain vasospastic angina and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Reperfusion injury
units.mechanism: Restoring oxygenated blood to injured myocardium can produce reactive oxygen species, calcium overload, and contraction band necrosis. Reperfusion may also transiently trigger arrhythmias despite its overall benefit.
units.case: After reopening an occluded coronary artery, injured myocytes show intensely eosinophilic transverse contraction bands.
units.pitfall: Reperfusion injury does not negate the benefit of promptly restoring flow to ischemic myocardium.
units.objective: Explain reperfusion injury and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Calcific aortic stenosis
units.mechanism: Progressive leaflet calcification restricts systolic opening and creates pressure overload in the LV. A crescendo–decrescendo systolic murmur radiating to the carotids and delayed carotid upstroke are classic findings.
units.case: An older adult has exertional syncope, angina, a late-peaking systolic ejection murmur, and a slow-rising carotid pulse.
units.pitfall: Murmur loudness alone does not grade stenosis; low flow may make severe obstruction sound softer.
units.objective: Explain calcific aortic stenosis and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Bicuspid aortic valve
units.mechanism: A congenitally two-cusped aortic valve undergoes accelerated mechanical stress and earlier calcification. It is associated with ascending aortic dilation and sometimes coarctation.
units.case: A middle-aged adult develops calcific outflow obstruction decades earlier than typical age-related degeneration and has ascending aortic dilation.
units.pitfall: Valve morphology and associated aortic disease are separate features that both require assessment.
units.objective: Explain bicuspid aortic valve and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Aortic regurgitation
units.mechanism: Incompetent aortic closure permits diastolic flow from the aorta into the LV, increasing volume load. Chronic disease may cause a dilated LV, wide pulse pressure, and an early diastolic decrescendo murmur.
units.case: A patient has bounding peripheral pulses and a high-pitched blowing murmur immediately after S2 along the left sternal border.
units.pitfall: Acute severe regurgitation may not produce the classic wide pulse pressure of chronic compensated disease.
units.objective: Explain aortic regurgitation and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Mitral regurgitation
units.mechanism: An incompetent mitral valve permits systolic LV-to-LA flow, creating a holosystolic murmur at the apex that often radiates to the axilla. Chronic volume overload enlarges the left atrium and ventricle.
units.case: An apical blowing systolic murmur extends from S1 to S2 and becomes louder with sustained handgrip.
units.pitfall: Acute severe regurgitation may occur without chamber enlargement because adaptation has not had time to develop.
units.objective: Explain mitral regurgitation and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Mitral stenosis
units.mechanism: Restricted mitral opening obstructs diastolic LA-to-LV flow, raising LA and pulmonary venous pressures. A low-pitched diastolic rumble and opening snap are characteristic of a mobile stenotic valve.
units.case: A patient with remote rheumatic fever has dyspnea, left atrial enlargement, and an opening snap followed by a diastolic rumble.
units.pitfall: Severe calcification may reduce leaflet mobility and eliminate the expected opening snap.
units.objective: Explain mitral stenosis and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Mitral valve prolapse
units.mechanism: Myxomatous leaflet degeneration allows systolic billowing into the left atrium, producing a midsystolic click with or without late systolic regurgitation. Reduced LV volume makes prolapse occur earlier in systole.
units.case: A click moves closer to S1 when a patient stands, and the associated late systolic murmur becomes longer.
units.pitfall: Most isolated prolapse is not a cause of severe hemodynamic compromise; the degree of regurgitation matters.
units.objective: Explain mitral valve prolapse and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Tricuspid regurgitation
units.mechanism: Systolic RV-to-RA backflow creates a holosystolic lower-left sternal murmur and prominent jugular v waves. Increased venous return during inspiration often augments the murmur.
units.case: A patient with right-sided endocarditis has a holosystolic murmur that becomes louder with inspiration and pulsatile neck veins.
units.pitfall: Respiratory augmentation supports a right-sided origin but is not an absolute rule in every patient.
units.objective: Explain tricuspid regurgitation and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Pulmonic stenosis
units.mechanism: Obstruction at the pulmonary valve raises RV systolic pressure and causes a systolic ejection murmur at the upper left sternal border. Congenital disease may produce an ejection click and delayed pulmonic closure.
units.case: A child has an upper-left sternal systolic ejection murmur and evidence of right ventricular pressure overload.
units.pitfall: Pulmonary flow murmurs from increased flow do not necessarily imply true valvular obstruction.
units.objective: Explain pulmonic stenosis and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Pulmonic regurgitation
units.mechanism: An incompetent pulmonary valve permits diastolic backflow into the RV. Severe pulmonary hypertension can cause a high-pitched early diastolic Graham Steell murmur at the upper left sternal border.
units.case: A patient with marked pulmonary hypertension develops a new early diastolic murmur in the pulmonary area.
units.pitfall: Aortic regurgitation can sound similar, so location, respiration, and associated findings are needed.
units.objective: Explain pulmonic regurgitation and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Physiologic S2 splitting
units.mechanism: Inspiration increases right-sided filling and delays pulmonic valve closure, while left-sided changes may bring aortic closure slightly earlier. The A2–P2 interval therefore widens with inspiration.
units.case: A healthy young adult has a second heart sound that splits during inspiration and becomes nearly single during expiration.
units.pitfall: Fixed, wide, and paradoxical splitting represent different mechanisms and should not be grouped together.
units.objective: Explain physiologic s2 splitting and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Paradoxical S2 splitting
units.mechanism: Delayed aortic valve closure can cause P2 to precede A2. Inspiration then delays P2 toward A2, narrowing the split; severe aortic stenosis and left bundle-branch block are classic settings.
units.case: A split second sound is audible in expiration but narrows on inspiration in a patient with delayed LV activation.
units.pitfall: Normal physiologic splitting widens with inspiration rather than narrowing.
units.objective: Explain paradoxical s2 splitting and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: S3 gallop
units.mechanism: Rapid early diastolic filling can generate an S3 when blood enters a dilated or volume-overloaded ventricle. It can be physiologic in younger people but suggests ventricular dysfunction in many older adults.
units.case: An older patient with dyspnea and a dilated LV has a low-frequency sound just after S2 during rapid filling.
units.pitfall: An S3 is not synonymous with heart failure in children, young adults, or pregnancy.
units.objective: Explain s3 gallop and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: S4 gallop
units.mechanism: Atrial contraction into a poorly compliant ventricle generates a late diastolic S4 just before S1. Chronic hypertension, ischemia, and hypertrophic disease are common settings.
units.case: A patient with concentric LV hypertrophy has an extra sound immediately before S1 that disappears when atrial fibrillation develops.
units.pitfall: An organized atrial contraction is required, so a true S4 is not expected during atrial fibrillation.
units.objective: Explain s4 gallop and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Handgrip maneuver
units.mechanism: Sustained isometric handgrip increases systemic vascular resistance and LV afterload. It usually increases regurgitant murmurs such as MR and AR and may reduce dynamic obstructive HCM intensity.
units.case: An apical holosystolic murmur becomes louder when the patient tightly grips both hands for a sustained interval.
units.pitfall: Maneuvers change loading conditions; they support, rather than replace, anatomic diagnosis.
units.objective: Explain handgrip maneuver and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Valsalva strain
units.mechanism: The strain phase reduces venous return and LV cavity size. Most flow-dependent murmurs soften, but obstructive HCM usually becomes louder and the prolapse click occurs earlier.
units.case: A systolic murmur intensifies when the patient strains against a closed glottis despite reduced ventricular filling.
units.pitfall: The release phase has different effects from the strain phase; identify which part of the maneuver is being described.
units.objective: Explain valsalva strain and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Squatting maneuver
units.mechanism: Squatting generally increases venous return and systemic vascular resistance. A larger LV cavity reduces dynamic HCM obstruction, while increased flow often augments an aortic stenosis murmur.
units.case: A dynamic systolic outflow murmur softens when a patient moves from standing to squatting.
units.pitfall: Simultaneous changes in preload and afterload mean no single variable explains every response.
units.objective: Explain squatting maneuver and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Inspiratory augmentation
units.mechanism: Inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure and increases systemic venous return, often increasing flow through right-sided valves. This explains classic inspiratory intensification of tricuspid regurgitation.
units.case: A lower sternal holosystolic murmur is more prominent during a deep breath in than during expiration.
units.pitfall: Left-sided murmurs do not universally disappear with inspiration, and severe right ventricular disease can alter the response.
units.objective: Explain inspiratory augmentation and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Opening snap severity relation
units.mechanism: In a mobile rheumatic stenotic mitral valve, higher LA pressure opens the valve earlier after aortic closure. A shorter A2-to-opening-snap interval therefore suggests more severe hemodynamic obstruction.
units.case: Two patients have mobile rheumatic mitral valves; the one with higher LA pressure has a shorter delay from A2 to the opening snap.
units.pitfall: The relationship is unreliable when calcification prevents a distinct opening snap.
units.objective: Explain opening snap severity relation and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Acute versus chronic regurgitation
units.mechanism: A sudden large regurgitant volume enters a chamber that has not developed compensatory dilation or compliance, sharply raising upstream pressures. Chronic regurgitation allows remodeling before decompensation.
units.case: A patient with sudden chordal rupture develops pulmonary edema despite a left atrium that is not enlarged.
units.pitfall: Absence of chronic chamber enlargement does not make acute severe valve regurgitation benign.
units.objective: Explain acute versus chronic regurgitation and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Functional mitral regurgitation
units.mechanism: LV dilation and papillary muscle displacement can tether otherwise nonprimary diseased mitral leaflets and enlarge the annulus. The regurgitation is secondary to ventricular remodeling rather than intrinsic leaflet damage.
units.case: A patient with dilated cardiomyopathy develops mitral leakage because displaced papillary muscles prevent proper leaflet coaptation.
units.pitfall: Primary leaflet disease and secondary ventricular geometry can produce the same direction of abnormal flow by different mechanisms.
units.objective: Explain functional mitral regurgitation and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: HFrEF
units.mechanism: Reduced LV systolic performance lowers ejection fraction and forward output. Ventricular dilation, elevated filling pressure, and neurohormonal activation may maintain circulation initially but can worsen remodeling and congestion over time.
units.case: A patient with prior myocardial injury has EF 30 percent, a dilated LV, pulmonary congestion, and exertional fatigue.
units.pitfall: Symptoms depend on loading and congestion as well as EF; the EF value alone does not describe the whole syndrome.
units.objective: Explain hfref and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: HFpEF
units.mechanism: A stiff or poorly relaxing LV requires increased filling pressure despite a preserved fraction of blood being ejected. Concentric hypertrophy, aging, obesity, and hypertension are common associated settings.
units.case: An older patient with long-standing hypertension has dyspnea, elevated LV filling pressure, concentric hypertrophy, and EF 60 percent.
units.pitfall: A normal EF does not demonstrate normal diastolic function or rule out heart failure.
units.objective: Explain hfpef and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Left-sided congestion
units.mechanism: Elevated LV filling pressure is transmitted to the left atrium and pulmonary veins, increasing pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure. Fluid can enter lung interstitium and alveoli, producing dyspnea and crackles.
units.case: A patient with LV failure develops orthopnea, pulmonary crackles, and interstitial edema from elevated pulmonary venous pressure.
units.pitfall: Pulmonary edema can also have noncardiogenic mechanisms, so lung fluid does not identify the cause by itself.
units.objective: Explain left-sided congestion and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Right-sided congestion
units.mechanism: Impaired RV forward flow raises systemic venous pressure, producing elevated JVP, hepatic congestion, peripheral edema, and sometimes ascites. Causes include left-sided failure, pulmonary hypertension, and primary RV disease.
units.case: A patient with RV dysfunction has distended neck veins, tender hepatomegaly, and dependent leg edema.
units.pitfall: Peripheral edema also occurs with renal, hepatic, and venous disorders and is not specific for RV failure.
units.objective: Explain right-sided congestion and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Neurohormonal remodeling
units.mechanism: Reduced effective arterial perfusion activates sympathetic pathways and RAAS. Vasoconstriction and sodium retention initially support pressure but increase cardiac load, fibrosis, and adverse ventricular remodeling with sustained activation.
units.case: A patient with chronic low-output failure develops elevated catecholamines, angiotensin II, and aldosterone with progressive fluid retention.
units.pitfall: A compensatory response that helps acutely may become harmful when persistently activated.
units.objective: Explain neurohormonal remodeling and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Natriuretic peptides
units.mechanism: Myocardial wall stretch stimulates release of natriuretic peptides, promoting natriuresis, vasodilation, and suppression of RAAS. BNP and NT-proBNP can support assessment of heart failure but are affected by age, kidney function, and body habitus.
units.case: Ventricular pressure and volume stress stimulate a hormone system that opposes sodium retention and vasoconstriction.
units.pitfall: An elevated peptide level is not uniquely diagnostic, and obesity can lower measured levels despite heart failure.
units.objective: Explain natriuretic peptides and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Dilated cardiomyopathy
units.mechanism: Chamber dilation with impaired systolic contraction produces reduced EF and secondary valve regurgitation. Genetic disease, toxins, viral injury, and metabolic causes can converge on this structural pattern.
units.case: Imaging shows a globally dilated hypokinetic LV without a single regional pattern explaining the dysfunction.
units.pitfall: A dilated phenotype is a structural description, not a complete etiologic diagnosis.
units.objective: Explain dilated cardiomyopathy and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Alcohol-associated cardiomyopathy
units.mechanism: Chronic heavy alcohol exposure can injure myocytes and impair contractile function, producing a dilated phenotype. The mechanism involves direct toxicity and metabolic effects, and nutritional deficiencies may coexist.
units.case: A patient with years of heavy alcohol use develops global systolic dysfunction and enlarged ventricular chambers.
units.pitfall: Alcohol exposure does not exclude another cause of cardiomyopathy; the differential remains broader than the history alone.
units.objective: Explain alcohol-associated cardiomyopathy and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Anthracycline cardiotoxicity
units.mechanism: Doxorubicin can cause dose-related myocardial injury through mechanisms including oxidative stress and topoisomerase IIβ-related damage. The result may be a dilated hypokinetic cardiomyopathy; dexrazoxane is cardioprotective in selected settings.
units.case: After cumulative anthracycline chemotherapy, a patient develops new global LV systolic dysfunction.
units.pitfall: Not all cancer-therapy cardiac toxicity has the same mechanism, reversibility, or timing.
units.objective: Explain anthracycline cardiotoxicity and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Peripartum cardiomyopathy
units.mechanism: Systolic heart failure arising late in pregnancy or in the months after delivery can occur without another identified cause. Proposed mechanisms include vascular and hormonal injury in a susceptible myocardium.
units.case: A previously healthy patient develops new reduced EF and heart failure shortly after delivery, with other causes excluded.
units.pitfall: Normal pregnancy causes hemodynamic changes but should not be used to dismiss new severe dyspnea or systolic dysfunction.
units.objective: Explain peripartum cardiomyopathy and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
units.mechanism: Often inherited sarcomeric mutations cause myocyte hypertrophy, fiber disarray, impaired relaxation, and sometimes dynamic outflow obstruction. Presentation can include exertional symptoms, arrhythmias, or sudden death.
units.case: A young adult with a family history of sudden death has asymmetric septal thickening and disorganized myocardial fibers.
units.pitfall: Hypertrophy from chronic hypertension or aortic stenosis is not automatically a primary sarcomeric disorder.
units.objective: Explain hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Dynamic LV outflow obstruction
units.mechanism: In obstructive HCM, septal hypertrophy and systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve narrow the LV outflow tract. Reduced preload or afterload and increased contractility can worsen the obstruction.
units.case: A systolic murmur becomes louder with standing or Valsalva strain as LV volume falls.
units.pitfall: Not every patient with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy has resting or provoked outflow obstruction.
units.objective: Explain dynamic lv outflow obstruction and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Restrictive cardiomyopathy
units.mechanism: Reduced ventricular compliance impairs diastolic filling, often with relatively preserved systolic function early and enlarged atria. Infiltrative or fibrotic processes cause high filling pressures without primary chamber dilation.
units.case: A patient has biatrial enlargement, high filling pressures, and relatively normal ventricular cavity size with impaired diastolic filling.
units.pitfall: Restrictive myocardial disease must be distinguished from a rigid pericardium because both can impair filling.
units.objective: Explain restrictive cardiomyopathy and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Cardiac amyloidosis
units.mechanism: Extracellular amyloid deposition thickens ventricular walls and impairs relaxation. Increased wall thickness on imaging may coexist with disproportionately low ECG voltage and systemic clues depending on amyloid type.
units.case: Echocardiography shows thick ventricular walls, but the ECG has low voltage in a patient with an infiltrative systemic disease.
units.pitfall: Wall thickening on imaging does not always represent hypertrophy of the myocytes themselves.
units.objective: Explain cardiac amyloidosis and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Cardiac hemochromatosis
units.mechanism: Iron deposition promotes oxidative injury and can cause conduction disease and restrictive or dilated cardiomyopathy. Systemic iron overload may also affect the liver, pancreas, skin, and joints.
units.case: A patient with diabetes, liver disease, and systemic iron overload develops heart failure and arrhythmias.
units.pitfall: The cardiac phenotype can change over time; iron overload is not limited to one fixed cardiomyopathy pattern.
units.objective: Explain cardiac hemochromatosis and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Cardiac sarcoidosis
units.mechanism: Noncaseating granulomatous inflammation can disrupt conduction tissue and ventricular myocardium, causing AV block, ventricular arrhythmias, and systolic dysfunction. Systemic pulmonary or skin findings may provide clues.
units.case: A relatively young adult with systemic noncaseating granulomatous disease develops unexplained high-grade AV block.
units.pitfall: Noncaseating granulomas are a pattern that requires context and exclusion of alternative causes.
units.objective: Explain cardiac sarcoidosis and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Chagas cardiomyopathy
units.mechanism: Trypanosoma cruzi infection can chronically damage myocardium and conduction tissue, producing dilated cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, and apical aneurysm. Gastrointestinal autonomic damage may coexist.
units.case: A patient with prior residence in rural Latin America develops cardiomyopathy, conduction abnormalities, and an apical ventricular aneurysm.
units.pitfall: Geographic exposure supports the diagnosis but should not substitute for appropriate confirmatory testing.
units.objective: Explain chagas cardiomyopathy and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Takotsubo syndrome
units.mechanism: Acute catecholamine-associated myocardial stunning can produce transient LV dysfunction, often with apical ballooning beyond a single coronary territory. It may follow emotional or physical stress and mimic an acute coronary syndrome.
units.case: After a major stressor, a patient has chest pain and transient apical ballooning without an obstructive coronary lesion explaining the pattern.
units.pitfall: It is an acute cardiac syndrome, not simply anxiety, and can cause significant complications.
units.objective: Explain takotsubo syndrome and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: High-output heart failure
units.mechanism: Markedly increased circulatory demand or reduced systemic resistance can require output beyond the heart's sustainable capacity, despite a high measured CO. Severe anemia, thyrotoxicosis, and large AV shunts are possible causes.
units.case: A patient with a large AV fistula develops congestion and tachycardia despite an elevated measured cardiac output.
units.pitfall: Heart failure describes an inadequate circulatory state and congestion, not invariably a low measured CO.
units.objective: Explain high-output heart failure and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy
units.mechanism: Sustained rapid rhythms can impair contractility and cause ventricular dilation through adverse loading, altered calcium handling, and energy imbalance. Function may improve when the arrhythmia is controlled.
units.case: A patient with persistent rapid atrial tachyarrhythmia develops global systolic dysfunction that improves after durable rate or rhythm control.
units.pitfall: Improvement supports the mechanism, but ischemic, genetic, and other causes should still be considered initially.
units.objective: Explain tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Ventricular septal defect
units.mechanism: A communication between ventricles usually produces left-to-right flow after pulmonary resistance falls. A small restrictive defect may generate a loud holosystolic murmur; a large defect can cause pulmonary overcirculation and heart failure.
units.case: An infant develops pulmonary overcirculation and a lower-left sternal holosystolic murmur after the postnatal decline in pulmonary vascular resistance.
units.pitfall: A louder murmur does not always mean a larger defect; small restrictive openings can be very turbulent.
units.objective: Explain ventricular septal defect and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Secundum atrial septal defect
units.mechanism: An opening in the region of the fossa ovalis allows predominantly left-to-right atrial flow, causing right-sided volume overload. Increased pulmonary flow produces an ejection murmur and fixed S2 splitting.
units.case: A young adult has right ventricular enlargement and fixed splitting of S2 with a pulmonary flow murmur.
units.pitfall: The typical murmur is from increased flow across the pulmonary valve, not from a high-velocity jet across the atrial opening.
units.objective: Explain secundum atrial septal defect and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Patent foramen ovale
units.mechanism: Failure of postnatal fusion between septal flaps leaves a potential atrial passage without a true deficiency of septal tissue. Transient right-to-left pressure gradients can permit paradoxical embolism.
units.case: An otherwise structurally normal atrial septum has unfused overlapping flaps that can open when right atrial pressure temporarily exceeds left atrial pressure.
units.pitfall: This common finding is anatomically different from a true atrial septal tissue defect.
units.objective: Explain patent foramen ovale and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Patent ductus arteriosus
units.mechanism: Persistence of the fetal aorta-to-pulmonary connection usually causes left-to-right flow after birth, producing continuous flow and a machinery murmur. Prematurity and congenital rubella are classic associations.
units.case: A premature infant has bounding pulses and a continuous murmur from flow between the aorta and pulmonary artery.
units.pitfall: In duct-dependent congenital lesions, maintaining the connection can be lifesaving rather than something to reverse immediately.
units.objective: Explain patent ductus arteriosus and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Ductal pharmacology
units.mechanism: Prostaglandin E helps maintain ductal patency, whereas cyclooxygenase inhibition reduces prostaglandin synthesis and can promote closure in suitable premature infants. The desired direction depends on the underlying lesion.
units.case: A newborn with a duct-dependent systemic circulation receives prostaglandin to preserve a fetal vascular connection until definitive care.
units.pitfall: A drug used to close an isolated PDA may be dangerous when circulation depends on that same ductus.
units.objective: Explain ductal pharmacology and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Tetralogy of Fallot
units.mechanism: Anterior displacement of the outflow septum produces RV outflow obstruction, VSD, overriding aorta, and secondary RV hypertrophy. The degree of obstruction strongly influences right-to-left shunting and cyanosis.
units.case: A child has a boot-shaped cardiac silhouette and cyanotic spells associated with a VSD and narrowed RV outflow tract.
units.pitfall: The four abnormalities are related consequences of a developmental outflow problem, not four independent acquired lesions.
units.objective: Explain tetralogy of fallot and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Tet spell physiology
units.mechanism: Reduced systemic resistance or increased RV outflow obstruction can increase right-to-left shunting in tetralogy of Fallot. Knee-chest positioning or squatting increases SVR and can improve pulmonary blood flow.
units.case: A cyanotic child spontaneously squats during exertion and becomes less blue as systemic vascular resistance rises.
units.pitfall: The maneuver improves shunt balance; it does not close the VSD or remove the anatomic outflow obstruction.
units.objective: Explain tet spell physiology and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Transposition of the great arteries
units.mechanism: Failure of normal outflow spiraling connects the aorta to the RV and pulmonary artery to the LV, creating parallel circulations. Survival requires mixing through an ASD, VSD, or PDA until correction.
units.case: A profoundly cyanotic newborn has separate systemic and pulmonary circuits and depends on an intercirculatory mixing site.
units.pitfall: Unlike a simple shunt lesion, inadequate mixing can cause severe cyanosis even when each ventricle ejects effectively.
units.objective: Explain transposition of the great arteries and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Persistent truncus arteriosus
units.mechanism: Failure of outflow septation leaves a single arterial trunk receiving blood from both ventricles, typically with a VSD. Mixed blood enters systemic and pulmonary circulations; increased pulmonary flow can cause heart failure.
units.case: A newborn has one common great arterial vessel arising above a ventricular septal defect.
units.pitfall: A single common outflow trunk is distinct from two separate but incorrectly connected great arteries.
units.objective: Explain persistent truncus arteriosus and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Tricuspid atresia
units.mechanism: Absence of a patent right atrioventricular connection prevents direct RA-to-RV flow, often leaving a hypoplastic RV. An atrial communication is required for systemic venous blood to leave the right atrium.
units.case: A cyanotic newborn has no functional right atrioventricular opening and must shunt blood across the atrial septum.
units.pitfall: Pulmonary blood flow depends on associated anatomy, so the lesion's physiology cannot be inferred from the absent valve alone.
units.objective: Explain tricuspid atresia and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Total anomalous pulmonary venous return
units.mechanism: Pulmonary veins connect to systemic venous structures instead of the left atrium. An atrial communication is required for blood to reach the left heart; venous obstruction can cause severe neonatal distress.
units.case: All pulmonary venous blood drains to the right-sided circulation, and an atrial opening is necessary for systemic output.
units.pitfall: Obstructed and unobstructed forms have different presentations and severity.
units.objective: Explain total anomalous pulmonary venous return and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Coarctation of the aorta
units.mechanism: A focal aortic narrowing, often near the ductal insertion, creates proximal hypertension and diminished distal perfusion. Collateral intercostal flow can cause rib notching in older patients.
units.case: A young person has high arm pressure, delayed femoral pulses, and lower leg pressure with enlarged collateral arteries.
units.pitfall: Neonatal critical obstruction may present when the ductus closes, before chronic collaterals have developed.
units.objective: Explain coarctation of the aorta and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Atrioventricular septal defect
units.mechanism: Abnormal endocardial cushion development can create combined atrial and ventricular septal defects with a common AV valve. The lesion is strongly associated with trisomy 21.
units.case: An infant with Down syndrome has a common atrioventricular valve and a defect spanning the lower atrial and inlet ventricular septa.
units.pitfall: An isolated secundum ASD does not represent the same developmental cushion defect.
units.objective: Explain atrioventricular septal defect and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Ebstein anomaly
units.mechanism: Apical displacement of tricuspid leaflets leads to atrialization of part of the RV and tricuspid regurgitation. Associated atrial shunting and accessory pathways may contribute to cyanosis or arrhythmia.
units.case: Imaging shows a tricuspid valve inserted unusually far toward the apex and a markedly enlarged right atrium.
units.pitfall: A maternal exposure association is not required for the diagnosis and does not establish causation in an individual case.
units.objective: Explain ebstein anomaly and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Hypoplastic left heart syndrome
units.mechanism: Severe underdevelopment of left-sided chambers and outflow structures prevents adequate independent systemic output. Systemic perfusion depends on flow from the pulmonary artery through a patent ductus.
units.case: A newborn deteriorates as the ductus constricts because the small left-sided structures cannot support systemic circulation.
units.pitfall: Closing the ductus in this setting worsens systemic perfusion instead of correcting a harmless extra connection.
units.objective: Explain hypoplastic left heart syndrome and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Neural crest contribution
units.mechanism: Cardiac neural crest cells contribute to conotruncal septation and aortic arch development. Disrupted migration or development can produce outflow and arch abnormalities, including those associated with 22q11.2 deletion.
units.case: A child with hypocalcemia and thymic hypoplasia also has a conotruncal cardiac defect.
units.pitfall: Many structures contribute to cardiac development; neural crest is especially important for outflow and arch patterning.
units.objective: Explain neural crest contribution and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Endocardial cushion development
units.mechanism: Cushions help form the atrioventricular septal complex and portions of the AV valves. Abnormal development produces characteristic inlet septal and valve abnormalities.
units.case: A developmental defect affects both AV valve formation and the septal tissue at the atrioventricular junction.
units.pitfall: Do not attribute every congenital septal defect to a single embryologic tissue without identifying its anatomic location.
units.objective: Explain endocardial cushion development and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Fetal circulatory shunts
units.mechanism: The ductus venosus bypasses much of the liver, the foramen ovale directs RA-to-LA flow, and the ductus arteriosus carries pulmonary arterial blood toward the aorta. These pathways support oxygen delivery before lung ventilation.
units.case: Before birth, highly oxygenated placental blood is preferentially directed across an atrial opening toward the left heart.
units.pitfall: Fetal flow directions differ from typical postnatal shunts because pulmonary resistance is high before birth.
units.objective: Explain fetal circulatory shunts and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Postnatal circulation transition
units.mechanism: Lung expansion lowers pulmonary vascular resistance while cord clamping increases systemic resistance. Increased pulmonary venous return raises LA pressure relative to RA pressure, functionally closing the foramen ovale.
units.case: After the first breaths, pulmonary flow increases and the atrial septal flap is pressed closed by higher left atrial pressure.
units.pitfall: Functional closure and permanent anatomic fusion occur on different timescales.
units.objective: Explain postnatal circulation transition and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Eisenmenger physiology
units.mechanism: A longstanding high-flow left-to-right shunt can cause pulmonary vascular remodeling and severe pulmonary hypertension. Once right-sided pressure exceeds systemic-side pressure, shunt reversal causes cyanosis and secondary erythrocytosis.
units.case: An adult with an unrepaired large congenital shunt develops late cyanosis after years of pulmonary vascular injury.
units.pitfall: Late closure of a defect after irreversible pulmonary vascular disease is not equivalent to early repair.
units.objective: Explain eisenmenger physiology and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Acute pericarditis
units.mechanism: Inflammation of the pericardial layers produces pleuritic positional pain and a friction rub. Diffuse ST elevation and PR depression may occur, reflecting inflammation rather than one occluded coronary territory.
units.case: Sharp chest pain improves when sitting forward and worsens lying flat, with diffuse ST elevation on ECG.
units.pitfall: Not every patient has all classic findings, and focal ischemia must still be considered when the presentation warrants it.
units.objective: Explain acute pericarditis and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Pericardial friction rub
units.mechanism: Inflamed pericardial surfaces moving against one another can generate a transient scratchy sound with components linked to cardiac motion. Leaning forward may improve detection at the left sternal border.
units.case: A clinician hears a superficial scratchy sound that persists when the patient briefly holds their breath.
units.pitfall: A pleural rub follows respiratory movement, whereas the pericardial sound is linked to cardiac movement.
units.objective: Explain pericardial friction rub and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Fibrinous pericarditis
units.mechanism: Fibrin deposition roughens pericardial surfaces and can produce the classic bread-and-butter gross appearance. Causes include postinfarction inflammation, uremia, autoimmune disease, and other injuries.
units.case: Gross examination after myocardial injury shows shaggy fibrin coating opposing pericardial surfaces.
units.pitfall: A morphologic pattern does not identify one exclusive cause; clinical timing and context determine the likely etiology.
units.objective: Explain fibrinous pericarditis and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Pericardial effusion
units.mechanism: Fluid accumulation in the pericardial space may be tolerated when gradual but can impair filling when rapid. Clinical effect depends on pressure-volume adaptation rather than fluid volume alone.
units.case: A slowly growing large effusion causes less circulatory compromise than a rapidly accumulating smaller traumatic effusion.
units.pitfall: A large cardiac silhouette does not establish tamponade, and an acute dangerous effusion may not enlarge the silhouette.
units.objective: Explain pericardial effusion and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Cardiac tamponade
units.mechanism: Elevated intrapericardial pressure restricts chamber filling and lowers stroke volume. Hypotension, raised JVP, muffled sounds, and exaggerated ventricular interdependence are classic manifestations.
units.case: After a penetrating chest injury, a patient becomes hypotensive with distended neck veins and impaired cardiac filling from rapidly accumulating pericardial blood.
units.pitfall: The classic triad is not always complete; absence of one component does not exclude the physiology.
units.objective: Explain cardiac tamponade and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Pulsus paradoxus
units.mechanism: An inspiratory fall in systolic pressure greater than 10 mmHg reflects exaggerated ventricular interdependence or respiratory hemodynamic variation. It is classically associated with tamponade but can also occur in severe obstructive airway disease.
units.case: During quiet inspiration, a patient's systolic pressure falls by 16 mmHg in the setting of a tense pericardial effusion.
units.pitfall: This sign is not unique to tamponade and must be interpreted with the full presentation.
units.objective: Explain pulsus paradoxus and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Electrical alternans
