units.mechanism: A large effusion can allow the heart to swing within the pericardial fluid, changing the orientation of electrical vectors and causing beat-to-beat QRS amplitude variation.
units.case: An ECG in a patient with a large effusion shows alternating tall and short QRS complexes from one beat to the next.
units.pitfall: Alternating amplitude supports the possibility of a large effusion but is neither universally present nor uniquely diagnostic.
units.objective: Explain electrical alternans and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Constrictive pericarditis
units.mechanism: A rigid scarred pericardium limits diastolic expansion and accentuates ventricular interdependence. Early rapid filling stops abruptly, producing elevated venous pressure and sometimes a pericardial knock.
units.case: A patient with prior pericardial injury has edema, elevated JVP, a calcified pericardium, and an early diastolic knock.
units.pitfall: Pericardial calcification is supportive but is not required for constriction.
units.objective: Explain constrictive pericarditis and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Kussmaul sign
units.mechanism: Failure of JVP to fall, or an actual rise during inspiration, indicates impaired accommodation of increased right-sided venous return. It can occur in constrictive pericarditis, restrictive cardiomyopathy, or RV infarction.
units.case: The neck veins become more prominent rather than less prominent during inspiration in a patient with limited RV filling.
units.pitfall: This response is not the typical defining sign of uncomplicated tamponade.
units.objective: Explain kussmaul sign and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Pericardial knock
units.mechanism: Abrupt cessation of early diastolic ventricular filling against a rigid pericardium can generate an early diastolic sound. It usually occurs earlier than a typical ventricular S3.
units.case: A patient with a scarred restrictive pericardial shell has a sharp sound soon after S2 as rapid filling is suddenly halted.
units.pitfall: A timing clue helps distinguish this sound from an opening snap or an S3, but imaging is needed for structural assessment.
units.objective: Explain pericardial knock and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Tamponade venous waveform
units.mechanism: Restricted filling throughout diastole blunts the right atrial y descent, while the x descent is often preserved or prominent. This differs from the rapid early filling and prominent y descent of constriction.
units.case: Venous pressure tracing in an obstructed pericardial sac shows a reduced y descent rather than brisk early diastolic emptying.
units.pitfall: Both tamponade and constriction can raise JVP, but their diastolic filling patterns differ.
units.objective: Explain tamponade venous waveform and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Constrictive versus restrictive disease
units.mechanism: Constriction is external pericardial limitation; restriction is intrinsic myocardial stiffness. Respiratory ventricular pressure discordance favors constriction, whereas concordant pressure changes more often support myocardial restriction.
units.case: During inspiration, invasive tracing shows RV systolic pressure rising while LV systolic pressure falls in a patient with impaired filling.
units.pitfall: No single bedside finding reliably distinguishes every case; combine physiology with imaging and clinical history.
units.objective: Explain constrictive versus restrictive disease and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Uremic pericarditis
units.mechanism: Advanced kidney failure can produce pericardial inflammation and a rub through retained metabolic factors. Typical diffuse ECG changes may be absent, and effusion can complicate the process.
units.case: A patient with severe renal dysfunction develops a friction rub and positional chest pain without classic diffuse ST elevation.
units.pitfall: Do not require a textbook ECG pattern to recognize pericardial inflammation in this setting.
units.objective: Explain uremic pericarditis and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Tuberculous pericarditis
units.mechanism: Mycobacterial infection can cause granulomatous pericardial inflammation, effusion, and later fibrotic constriction. Epidemiology and systemic infection features help guide the differential.
units.case: A patient with tuberculosis develops a chronic pericardial effusion followed by a thickened constrictive pericardial shell.
units.pitfall: Tuberculosis is an important global cause, but not all chronic constrictive disease is infectious.
units.objective: Explain tuberculous pericarditis and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Malignant pericardial effusion
units.mechanism: Tumor spread or related lymphatic obstruction can produce persistent, sometimes hemorrhagic pericardial fluid. Hemodynamic consequences depend on the rate of accumulation and pericardial pressure.
units.case: A patient with metastatic lung cancer develops a recurrent bloody pericardial effusion.
units.pitfall: Blood in the pericardium is not specific to malignancy; trauma and other causes also produce hemorrhagic fluid.
units.objective: Explain malignant pericardial effusion and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Viral myocarditis
units.mechanism: Inflammatory myocardial injury after viral infection can involve direct injury and immune mechanisms, causing chest pain, arrhythmias, troponin elevation, or systolic dysfunction. Biopsy may show lymphocytic infiltrates with myocyte injury.
units.case: A young adult develops heart failure and arrhythmias after a viral syndrome, with lymphocytes surrounding damaged myocytes.
units.pitfall: A preceding viral illness is suggestive but does not prove a specific pathogen caused the myocardial injury.
units.objective: Explain viral myocarditis and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Giant cell myocarditis
units.mechanism: An aggressive inflammatory myocardial disorder with multinucleated giant cells and myocyte necrosis can cause rapidly progressive heart failure, ventricular arrhythmias, and conduction disease.
units.case: Rapidly worsening cardiac failure is associated with biopsy evidence of multinucleated giant cells and extensive myocyte destruction.
units.pitfall: This destructive pattern differs from well-formed noncaseating granulomas typical of sarcoidosis.
units.objective: Explain giant cell myocarditis and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Hypersensitivity myocarditis
units.mechanism: Drug-related immune reactions can produce eosinophil-rich myocardial inflammation. A temporal relationship to a new medication and systemic hypersensitivity findings may provide clues.
units.case: After starting a new drug, a patient develops rash, eosinophilia, and myocardial inflammation dominated by eosinophils.
units.pitfall: Eosinophilic myocardial disease has other causes, so the medication history is part of the assessment rather than proof alone.
units.objective: Explain hypersensitivity myocarditis and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Diphtheritic myocarditis
units.mechanism: Corynebacterium diphtheriae toxin inactivates elongation factor 2 by ADP-ribosylation, inhibiting protein synthesis. Systemic toxin injury can damage myocardium and conduction tissue after respiratory infection.
units.case: An inadequately immunized patient with a pharyngeal pseudomembrane develops arrhythmia and myocardial dysfunction from a circulating toxin.
units.pitfall: Cardiac damage is toxin-mediated and can develop even when the initial respiratory focus seems localized.
units.objective: Explain diphtheritic myocarditis and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Immune checkpoint myocarditis
units.mechanism: Cancer immune checkpoint blockade can trigger immune-mediated myocardial injury, sometimes with conduction disease and overlapping myositis. The mechanism is enhanced immune activation rather than cumulative anthracycline toxicity.
units.case: Soon after immune checkpoint treatment, a patient develops elevated troponin, AV block, and muscle weakness.
units.pitfall: Different anticancer therapies can injure the heart through very different pathways and require mechanism-specific evaluation.
units.objective: Explain immune checkpoint myocarditis and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Primary hypertension
units.mechanism: Common chronic hypertension arises from interacting genetic, renal, vascular, and environmental factors rather than one identifiable lesion. Sustained pressure promotes vascular injury and cardiac remodeling over time.
units.case: An adult develops persistent hypertension without a clear endocrine or renovascular cause, with a family history and multiple lifestyle risk factors.
units.pitfall: The absence of a secondary cause does not make the long-term vascular consequences trivial.
units.objective: Explain primary hypertension and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Renovascular hypertension
units.mechanism: Reduced renal perfusion stimulates renin release, angiotensin II formation, and aldosterone secretion. Atherosclerotic renal artery narrowing or fibromuscular dysplasia can initiate this secondary pressure elevation.
units.case: A patient with renal artery narrowing has elevated renin and aldosterone driven by perceived low renal perfusion.
units.pitfall: Both aldosterone and renin are generally high, unlike primary aldosterone excess where renin is suppressed.
units.objective: Explain renovascular hypertension and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Primary aldosteronism
units.mechanism: Autonomous aldosterone secretion increases sodium retention and potassium and hydrogen loss while suppressing renin. Hypertension with hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis is a classic pattern, although potassium may be normal.
units.case: A hypertensive patient has high aldosterone, low renin, and unexplained potassium depletion.
units.pitfall: Normal potassium does not exclude this diagnosis, and the ratio requires careful interpretation in the context of medications.
units.objective: Explain primary aldosteronism and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Pheochromocytoma
units.mechanism: Catecholamine secretion from chromaffin cells can cause episodic or sustained hypertension, palpitations, headache, and sweating. α-mediated vasoconstriction and β-mediated cardiac effects drive the hemodynamic features.
units.case: Paroxysms of headache, diaphoresis, and palpitations occur with marked blood pressure surges and elevated catecholamine metabolites.
units.pitfall: If receptor blockade is used, isolated β blockade before adequate α blockade can worsen vasoconstriction.
units.objective: Explain pheochromocytoma and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis
units.mechanism: Plasma protein leakage and smooth-muscle matrix deposition thicken small-vessel walls and narrow their lumens. Chronic hypertension and diabetes are classic associated conditions.
units.case: Renal arterioles in a patient with long-standing hypertension have homogeneous pink wall thickening with narrowed lumens.
units.pitfall: This chronic glassy pattern differs from the concentric cellular onion-skin change of severe pressure injury.
units.objective: Explain hyaline arteriolosclerosis and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis
units.mechanism: Severe hypertension can stimulate concentric smooth-muscle proliferation and basement membrane duplication, creating an onion-skin appearance. Fibrinoid necrosis may coexist in acute severe vascular injury.
units.case: A patient with very high pressure and acute organ injury has renal arterioles showing concentric laminated wall thickening.
units.pitfall: Severe hypertension is a clinical syndrome of pressure and organ injury; histology is not needed to recognize an emergency.
units.objective: Explain hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Atherosclerotic plaque formation
units.mechanism: Endothelial dysfunction promotes lipid entry, LDL modification, monocyte recruitment, and foam-cell formation. Smooth-muscle migration and extracellular matrix create a fibrous cap over a lipid-rich core.
units.case: An arterial intimal lesion contains macrophage foam cells, cholesterol material, and a collagenous cap.
units.pitfall: Atherosclerosis affects the intima of large and medium arteries rather than simply being a small-vessel wall thickening.
units.objective: Explain atherosclerotic plaque formation and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Plaque vulnerability
units.mechanism: A thin fibrous cap, large lipid core, and inflammatory activity increase the chance of plaque disruption. Macrophage proteases can weaken cap collagen and expose thrombogenic material when the surface breaks.
units.case: A coronary plaque with modest prior narrowing ruptures because of a large lipid core and inflamed thin cap.
units.pitfall: The most severely stenotic plaque is not necessarily the one most likely to rupture.
units.objective: Explain plaque vulnerability and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Aortic dissection
units.mechanism: A tear permits blood to separate layers of the aortic media, forming a false lumen. Hypertension and connective tissue disease predispose; branch compromise, tamponade, or aortic regurgitation may complicate proximal disease.
units.case: A hypertensive patient develops sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back with unequal peripheral pulses.
units.pitfall: A dissection separates wall layers and is anatomically different from a full-thickness ruptured aneurysm.
units.objective: Explain aortic dissection and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Abdominal aortic aneurysm
units.mechanism: Degeneration and weakening of the infrarenal aortic wall cause progressive dilation. Smoking is a major risk factor, and rupture risk increases with larger size and rapid growth.
units.case: An older smoker has an enlarging infrarenal pulsatile aortic dilation with mural thrombus.
units.pitfall: A mural thrombus does not eliminate rupture risk, and most aneurysms do not announce themselves with the full classic symptom triad.
units.objective: Explain abdominal aortic aneurysm and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Marfan aortopathy
units.mechanism: FBN1-related connective tissue dysfunction and altered matrix signaling predispose to aortic root dilation, regurgitation, and dissection. Skeletal and ocular findings support the systemic diagnosis.
units.case: A tall patient with ectopia lentis and long extremities develops progressive aortic root enlargement.
units.pitfall: Body habitus alone does not establish the disorder; the cardiovascular and systemic pattern is essential.
units.objective: Explain marfan aortopathy and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Giant cell arteritis
units.mechanism: Granulomatous large- and medium-vessel inflammation often affects branches of the carotid artery in older adults. New headache, jaw claudication, and visual symptoms are characteristic warning features.
units.case: An older adult has new temporal headache, pain while chewing, high inflammatory markers, and transient monocular vision loss.
units.pitfall: The disease can involve the aorta as well as cranial branches; a normal-feeling temporal artery does not exclude it.
units.objective: Explain giant cell arteritis and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Takayasu arteritis
units.mechanism: Granulomatous inflammation of the aorta and major branches can cause stenosis and unequal limb perfusion. Younger patients may present with reduced upper-limb pulses, bruits, and pressure discrepancies.
units.case: A young adult has arm claudication, weak upper-extremity pulses, and narrowing of major aortic branches.
units.pitfall: Age and distribution help distinguish this pattern from other large-vessel vasculitides but are not absolute by themselves.
units.objective: Explain takayasu arteritis and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Polyarteritis nodosa
units.mechanism: Necrotizing inflammation of medium muscular arteries causes segmental injury, microaneurysms, and organ ischemia. Renal and gastrointestinal involvement are common, while pulmonary capillaritis is not a typical feature.
units.case: A patient has abdominal pain, hypertension from renal ischemia, and angiographic medium-artery microaneurysms with spared pulmonary capillaries.
units.pitfall: This pattern differs from small-vessel vasculitis that directly affects glomeruli and lung capillaries.
units.objective: Explain polyarteritis nodosa and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Kawasaki disease
units.mechanism: A childhood medium-vessel vasculitis can damage coronary arteries and produce aneurysms. Prolonged fever with conjunctival, oral, rash, extremity, and cervical node findings supports recognition.
units.case: A child with persistent fever, strawberry tongue, conjunctivitis, and swollen hands later develops coronary artery dilation.
units.pitfall: The major cardiac concern is coronary involvement, not simply the duration or height of fever.
units.objective: Explain kawasaki disease and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Thromboangiitis obliterans
units.mechanism: A tobacco-associated inflammatory thrombotic disease affects small and medium extremity vessels. Distal ischemia, superficial thrombophlebitis, and ischemic digits can occur in younger smokers.
units.case: A young heavy smoker develops painful ischemic fingers and toes with segmental thrombosis of distal vessels.
units.pitfall: This is not merely early large-artery atherosclerosis; the distal inflammatory thrombotic pattern is distinctive.
units.objective: Explain thromboangiitis obliterans and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Raynaud phenomenon
units.mechanism: Episodic vasospasm of digital arteries produces color changes triggered by cold or emotional stress. Primary disease lacks an underlying systemic disorder; secondary disease can accompany connective tissue disease.
units.case: Cold exposure triggers sharply demarcated pale then blue digits followed by redness during rewarming.
units.pitfall: The full three-color sequence is not always present, and digital ulceration raises concern for secondary disease.
units.objective: Explain raynaud phenomenon and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Peripheral arterial disease
units.mechanism: Atherosclerotic flow limitation causes exertional muscle ischemia, classically reproducible leg pain relieved by rest. Reduced ankle systolic pressure compared with arm pressure supports the diagnosis.
units.case: Calf discomfort occurs after a predictable walking distance and resolves with rest; pedal pulses are diminished.
units.pitfall: A normal or high ankle–brachial ratio can be misleading with noncompressible calcified arteries, especially in diabetes or kidney disease.
units.objective: Explain peripheral arterial disease and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Cholesterol embolization
units.mechanism: Dislodged atheromatous debris lodges in small arteries, causing tissue ischemia and inflammation. It can follow vascular procedures and present with blue toes, livedo reticularis, and renal dysfunction.
units.case: After aortic instrumentation, a patient develops painful blue toes with palpable larger pulses and worsening kidney function.
units.pitfall: Palpable peripheral pulses do not exclude microvascular occlusion by embolic debris.
units.objective: Explain cholesterol embolization and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Aortic arch embryology
units.mechanism: The third arch contributes to carotid arteries, the fourth to portions of the aortic arch and right subclavian, and the sixth to pulmonary arteries and the left ductus arteriosus. Remodeling errors create recognizable arch anomalies.
units.case: A developmental question asks which arch contributes to the fetal connection between the pulmonary artery and descending aorta; the answer is the left sixth arch.
units.pitfall: Adult aortic anatomy emerges from selective persistence and regression, not from one unchanged symmetric embryonic vessel.
units.objective: Explain aortic arch embryology and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: ACE inhibitors
units.mechanism: Blocking angiotensin-converting enzyme reduces angiotensin II and aldosterone and decreases bradykinin breakdown. Effects include reduced vascular tone and sodium retention; adverse effects include cough, angioedema, hyperkalemia, and fetal toxicity.
units.case: A patient develops a persistent dry cough after starting a pressure-lowering drug that increases bradykinin and lowers angiotensin II formation.
units.pitfall: These agents are avoided in pregnancy and can reduce filtration in settings where angiotensin-dependent efferent constriction is maintaining GFR.
units.objective: Explain ace inhibitors and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Angiotensin receptor blockers
units.mechanism: AT1 receptor blockade inhibits angiotensin II-mediated vasoconstriction and aldosterone release without directly inhibiting bradykinin degradation. Hyperkalemia and fetal toxicity remain important risks, but cough is less common than with ACE inhibition.
units.case: A patient who cannot tolerate an ACE inhibitor because of cough receives an agent that blocks angiotensin II at its receptor instead.
units.pitfall: Avoiding bradykinin accumulation does not remove the potassium, pregnancy, or renal hemodynamic concerns of RAAS blockade.
units.objective: Explain angiotensin receptor blockers and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Renin inhibition
units.mechanism: Aliskiren directly inhibits renin and reduces formation of angiotensin I, acting upstream of ACE. Suppression of the RAAS can cause hyperkalemia and fetal toxicity, and combinations with other RAAS blockers carry important restrictions.
units.case: A pharmacology experiment blocks conversion of angiotensinogen to angiotensin I rather than blocking ACE or the AT1 receptor.
units.pitfall: An upstream target does not make combined RAAS blockade automatically safer or more effective.
units.objective: Explain renin inhibition and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Mineralocorticoid antagonists
units.mechanism: Spironolactone and eplerenone inhibit aldosterone action, reducing sodium retention and potassium excretion. Spironolactone also interacts with sex-steroid receptors and can cause gynecomastia; both can cause hyperkalemia.
units.case: A patient develops breast tenderness and elevated potassium after treatment targeting the aldosterone receptor.
units.pitfall: Eplerenone is more selective for the mineralocorticoid receptor but still carries hyperkalemia risk.
units.objective: Explain mineralocorticoid antagonists and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Beta blockers
units.mechanism: β receptor antagonism lowers heart rate, contractility, and renin release. Selected agents benefit chronic HFrEF, but negative inotropy and chronotropy can worsen acute low-output states or conduction block.
units.case: A drug lowers myocardial oxygen demand and slows AV conduction by reducing adrenergic stimulation of the heart.
units.pitfall: Benefits in stable chronic heart failure do not mean the same drug should be newly escalated during hemodynamic collapse.
units.objective: Explain beta blockers and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Dihydropyridine calcium blockers
units.mechanism: Agents such as amlodipine inhibit L-type calcium channels predominantly in vascular smooth muscle, causing arteriolar dilation. Peripheral edema, flushing, and headache are common; rapid-acting vasodilation can produce reflex tachycardia.
units.case: A pressure-lowering drug relaxes arterioles and causes ankle edema without directly slowing AV nodal conduction to the extent of verapamil.
units.pitfall: The edema can reflect altered capillary hydrostatic forces rather than generalized excess total-body fluid.
units.objective: Explain dihydropyridine calcium blockers and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Non-dihydropyridine calcium blockers
units.mechanism: Verapamil and diltiazem inhibit L-type calcium channels in the AV node and myocardium, slowing conduction and reducing contractility. Bradycardia and AV block are important risks; verapamil commonly causes constipation.
units.case: A patient has PR prolongation and constipation after a medication that acts on AV nodal calcium channels.
units.pitfall: Combining nodal blockers increases bradycardia risk, and negative inotropy is problematic in systolic heart failure.
units.objective: Explain non-dihydropyridine calcium blockers and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Organic nitrates
units.mechanism: Nitric oxide signaling activates guanylyl cyclase and raises cGMP, relaxing vascular smooth muscle. Venodilation reduces preload and wall stress; headache, hypotension, tolerance, and interaction with PDE5 inhibitors are central adverse-effect concepts.
units.case: A patient develops profound hypotension after combining sildenafil with a drug that supplies nitric oxide for angina relief.
units.pitfall: The cGMP interaction can be dangerous even when each drug was tolerated separately.
units.objective: Explain organic nitrates and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Hydralazine
units.mechanism: Direct arteriolar relaxation reduces afterload and can provoke reflex tachycardia and fluid retention. Drug-induced lupus is a classic adverse effect, especially with prolonged exposure in susceptible patients.
units.case: A patient receiving an arteriolar dilator develops arthralgia and antinuclear antibodies with a lupus-like syndrome.
units.pitfall: Its predominantly arteriolar action differs from nitrate venodilation; the two act on different loading components.
units.objective: Explain hydralazine and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Sodium nitroprusside
units.mechanism: This nitric oxide donor rapidly dilates both arteries and veins through cGMP. Metabolism can produce cyanide, while thiocyanate accumulates especially with impaired renal clearance during prolonged exposure.
units.case: During a prolonged infusion of a potent balanced vasodilator, a patient develops evidence of impaired cellular oxygen utilization and metabolic acidosis.
units.pitfall: Cyanide and thiocyanate toxicity are related but distinct metabolic concerns, with different contributing risk factors.
units.objective: Explain sodium nitroprusside and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Loop diuretics
units.mechanism: Inhibition of NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb produces strong natriuresis and reduces the medullary concentration gradient. Adverse effects include hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, volume depletion, and ototoxicity; calcium excretion increases.
units.case: A diuretic blocks luminal Na–K–2Cl transport in the thick ascending limb and increases urinary calcium loss.
units.pitfall: Potassium depletion can increase arrhythmia risk and susceptibility to digoxin toxicity.
units.objective: Explain loop diuretics and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Thiazide diuretics
units.mechanism: Inhibition of the Na–Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule increases sodium excretion and promotes calcium reabsorption. Hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hyperuricemia, and altered glucose handling are notable adverse effects.
units.case: A pressure-lowering diuretic reduces urinary calcium but can precipitate gout and lower serum sodium.
units.pitfall: Its calcium effect is opposite to that of loop diuretics; both can cause potassium loss.
units.objective: Explain thiazide diuretics and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: ENaC blockers
units.mechanism: Amiloride and triamterene inhibit epithelial sodium channels in the collecting duct, reducing the lumen-negative potential that favors potassium secretion. They are potassium-sparing and can cause hyperkalemia.
units.case: A collecting-duct drug directly blocks luminal sodium entry rather than antagonizing the intracellular aldosterone receptor.
units.pitfall: Potassium sparing does not mean risk free: kidney dysfunction and concurrent RAAS blockade increase hyperkalemia risk.
units.objective: Explain enac blockers and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Digoxin
units.mechanism: Na/K ATPase inhibition increases intracellular sodium, reduces Na/Ca exchange-mediated calcium extrusion, and increases contractile calcium availability. Vagal effects slow AV conduction; toxicity can cause nausea, visual changes, and multiple arrhythmias.
units.case: A patient with kidney dysfunction and low potassium develops nausea, yellow-tinged vision, and arrhythmias while taking a positive inotropic glycoside.
units.pitfall: Dose-related toxicity is influenced by renal function and electrolytes; a heart-rate response alone does not establish safety.
units.objective: Explain digoxin and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: SGLT2 inhibitors
units.mechanism: Blocking proximal tubular sodium–glucose cotransport promotes glycosuria and natriuresis. These agents have heart failure benefits beyond glucose lowering; important adverse effects include genital fungal infection and euglycemic ketoacidosis.
units.case: A patient treated for heart failure develops a high-anion-gap ketoacidosis despite only modest blood glucose elevation while using a proximal tubular glucose-transport inhibitor.
units.pitfall: Near-normal glucose does not exclude ketoacidosis in a patient taking this drug class.
units.objective: Explain sglt2 inhibitors and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Neprilysin inhibition
units.mechanism: Sacubitril reduces degradation of natriuretic peptides and is paired with valsartan to limit angiotensin receptor signaling. Enhanced natriuretic pathways reduce cardiac load; angioedema and hyperkalemia remain relevant risks.
units.case: A heart failure combination augments natriuretic peptides while blocking AT1 receptors rather than inhibiting ACE.
units.pitfall: Concurrent ACE inhibition is avoided and a washout is required because overlapping bradykinin effects increase angioedema risk.
units.objective: Explain neprilysin inhibition and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Statins
units.mechanism: HMG-CoA reductase inhibition reduces hepatic cholesterol synthesis and upregulates hepatic LDL receptors. Myalgia, rare severe myopathy, and liver enzyme changes are key adverse-effect concepts; interactions can raise exposure.
units.case: A lipid-lowering drug decreases mevalonate synthesis and increases hepatic clearance of circulating LDL particles.
units.pitfall: A fall in LDL reflects both synthesis inhibition and receptor upregulation, not direct removal of cholesterol from blood by the drug.
units.objective: Explain statins and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Ezetimibe and PCSK9 inhibition
units.mechanism: Ezetimibe blocks intestinal NPC1L1-mediated cholesterol uptake, whereas PCSK9 inhibitors preserve hepatic LDL receptor recycling. Both lower LDL through mechanisms distinct from inhibiting cholesterol synthesis.
units.case: Two adjunctive lipid therapies act at intestinal cholesterol uptake and hepatic LDL receptor degradation, respectively.
units.pitfall: Different targets can complement statin action; do not assign the same synthesis-blocking mechanism to all LDL-lowering agents.
units.objective: Explain ezetimibe and pcsk9 inhibition and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Antiplatelet drugs
units.mechanism: Aspirin irreversibly inhibits platelet cyclooxygenase and thromboxane synthesis, while P2Y12 inhibitors block ADP-mediated platelet activation. Both target platelet-dependent arterial thrombosis but increase bleeding risk.
units.case: A coronary thrombosis prevention regimen combines suppression of thromboxane generation with blockade of the platelet ADP receptor.
units.pitfall: Antiplatelet mechanisms differ from anticoagulation even when both are used in a vascular disease setting.
units.objective: Explain antiplatelet drugs and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Anticoagulants
units.mechanism: Heparin potentiates antithrombin, warfarin reduces vitamin K-dependent factor activation, direct Xa inhibitors inhibit factor Xa, and dabigatran inhibits thrombin. Their onset, monitoring, elimination, and reversal strategies differ.
units.case: A pharmacology comparison distinguishes antithrombin activation from inhibition of vitamin K recycling and direct inhibition of factor Xa or thrombin.
units.pitfall: Drugs grouped as anticoagulants are not interchangeable, and an INR is not a universal measure of their effect.
units.objective: Explain anticoagulants and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Class IA action
units.mechanism: Quinidine, procainamide, and disopyramide moderately block fast sodium channels and also prolong repolarization. They can widen QRS and lengthen QT, creating a risk of torsades.
units.case: A rhythm drug moderately slows ventricular conduction and lengthens the action potential through additional potassium-channel effects.
units.pitfall: The class label predicts an electrophysiologic tendency, not identical adverse effects for every member.
units.objective: Explain class ia action and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Quinidine adverse effects
units.mechanism: Quinidine can cause cinchonism with tinnitus, headache, and dizziness, as well as diarrhea and QT-related arrhythmia risk. Its class IA action combines sodium-channel blockade with prolonged repolarization.
units.case: A patient taking an older rhythm-control agent develops tinnitus, dizziness, and a prolonged QT interval.
units.pitfall: Tinnitus is a useful drug association but does not replace checking electrolytes and other causes of QT prolongation.
units.objective: Explain quinidine adverse effects and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Procainamide adverse effects
units.mechanism: Procainamide is a class IA agent associated with drug-induced lupus and, less commonly, hematologic toxicity. Its active metabolite also prolongs repolarization, especially relevant when clearance is impaired.
units.case: Months after starting a class IA drug, a patient develops arthralgia and a lupus-like serologic pattern.
units.pitfall: Drug-induced lupus typically has a different organ involvement pattern from spontaneous systemic lupus, though overlap can occur.
units.objective: Explain procainamide adverse effects and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Disopyramide adverse effects
units.mechanism: Disopyramide is a class IA sodium-channel blocker with prominent antimuscarinic and negative inotropic effects. Urinary retention, dry mouth, and worsening pump dysfunction are important pharmacologic associations.
units.case: An older patient develops dry mouth and difficulty urinating after a rhythm drug with strong anticholinergic activity.
units.pitfall: Its negative inotropy is not a generic benefit in every cardiac patient, even though selected obstructive physiology can exploit it.
units.objective: Explain disopyramide adverse effects and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Class IB action
units.mechanism: Lidocaine and mexiletine preferentially affect inactivated sodium channels and have greater effects in depolarized or ischemic ventricular tissue. They tend to shorten ventricular action potential duration rather than prolong QT.
units.case: A sodium-channel blocker is most effective in ischemic ventricular myocardium and shortens rather than lengthens action potential duration.
units.pitfall: Sodium-channel blockers differ substantially by binding kinetics and effects on repolarization.
units.objective: Explain class ib action and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Lidocaine toxicity
units.mechanism: Systemic lidocaine toxicity can cause neurologic symptoms such as paresthesias, confusion, tremor, and seizures, with cardiovascular toxicity at higher exposure. It is a class IB agent rather than a primary AV nodal blocker.
units.case: During administration of a ventricular sodium-channel blocker, a patient develops perioral numbness and seizures.
units.pitfall: Route, dose, tissue uptake, and impaired clearance influence toxicity; local anesthetic use can also produce systemic exposure.
units.objective: Explain lidocaine toxicity and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Mexiletine
units.mechanism: Mexiletine is an orally active class IB sodium-channel blocker with ventricular electrophysiologic effects similar to lidocaine. Gastrointestinal upset and neurologic adverse effects are important limitations.
units.case: An oral analog of a class IB ventricular antiarrhythmic causes nausea and tremor while having relatively little QT-prolonging effect.
units.pitfall: An oral route does not change the underlying sodium-channel class or eliminate neurologic toxicity.
units.objective: Explain mexiletine and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Class IC action
units.mechanism: Flecainide and propafenone strongly slow fast sodium-dependent conduction with relatively little direct effect on action potential duration. Marked QRS widening and proarrhythmia are concerns, particularly with structural or ischemic heart disease.
units.case: A rhythm drug markedly prolongs ventricular conduction but has relatively little primary effect on repolarization duration.
units.pitfall: Strong suppression of ectopy does not guarantee improved outcomes in patients with infarct-related structural disease.
units.objective: Explain class ic action and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Use-dependent sodium block
units.mechanism: Many sodium-channel blockers bind more effectively when channels repeatedly open or enter inactivated states. Faster rates can therefore intensify conduction slowing, especially with slowly dissociating class IC drugs.
units.case: A patient's QRS becomes wider at faster heart rates while taking a sodium-channel blocker that dissociates slowly.
units.pitfall: Drug effect can change with rate even when the serum concentration is stable.
units.objective: Explain use-dependent sodium block and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Class II antiarrhythmics
units.mechanism: β blockade reduces cAMP-mediated nodal calcium currents and sympathetic automaticity, slowing sinus rate and AV conduction. PR prolongation can occur, while excessive blockade causes bradycardia or AV block.
units.case: A rhythm-control drug blunts sympathetic AV nodal stimulation and prolongs PR rather than primarily widening QRS.
units.pitfall: Combining multiple AV nodal suppressants can produce additive conduction slowing.
units.objective: Explain class ii antiarrhythmics and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Class III action
units.mechanism: Potassium-channel blockade prolongs phase 3 repolarization and effective refractory period. Many members prolong QT and can cause torsades, although the degree of proarrhythmic risk differs across drugs.
units.case: A drug increases ventricular action potential duration by reducing outward potassium current during repolarization.
units.pitfall: A long QT is a risk marker, but different drugs do not carry identical torsades risk.
units.objective: Explain class iii action and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Amiodarone mechanisms
units.mechanism: Amiodarone has potassium-, sodium-, calcium-channel and β-blocking effects. It prolongs repolarization but is not a selective single-channel drug, and its tissue accumulation produces a long and variable elimination period.
units.case: A rhythm drug displays properties of several antiarrhythmic classes and can have effects persisting long after discontinuation.
units.pitfall: Its multichannel action and long tissue residence make simple one-target comparisons incomplete.
units.objective: Explain amiodarone mechanisms and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Amiodarone organ toxicity
units.mechanism: Amiodarone can cause pulmonary injury, thyroid dysfunction, liver injury, corneal deposits, and skin discoloration. Its iodine content contributes to either hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism in different settings.
units.case: A patient on chronic therapy develops dyspnea from interstitial lung injury together with abnormal thyroid tests.
units.pitfall: Corneal microdeposits are common and are not equivalent to every form of serious visual toxicity.
units.objective: Explain amiodarone organ toxicity and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Sotalol
units.mechanism: Sotalol combines nonselective β blockade with class III potassium-channel effects, so it can slow rate and prolong QT. Reduced renal clearance can increase exposure and proarrhythmic risk.
units.case: A single rhythm drug causes bradycardia through β blockade and also lengthens QT through potassium-channel inhibition.
units.pitfall: Its β-blocking component does not eliminate the possibility of torsades from prolonged repolarization.
units.objective: Explain sotalol and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Dofetilide and ibutilide
units.mechanism: These agents prolong atrial and ventricular repolarization through class III effects and can be used in selected atrial rhythm-conversion settings. QT prolongation and torsades are central safety concerns.
units.case: An atrial rhythm-conversion drug prolongs repolarization without relying mainly on AV nodal blockade, requiring close QT assessment.
units.pitfall: Electrolyte abnormalities and other QT-prolonging drugs can amplify the arrhythmia risk.
units.objective: Explain dofetilide and ibutilide and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Class IV antiarrhythmics
units.mechanism: Verapamil and diltiazem slow calcium-dependent AV nodal conduction and increase nodal refractoriness. Their negative chronotropic and inotropic effects distinguish them from primarily vascular dihydropyridines.
units.case: A regular AV node-dependent tachycardia is slowed by a calcium-channel blocker that prolongs the PR interval.
units.pitfall: These effects do not make AV nodal blockers safe for pre-excited atrial fibrillation.
units.objective: Explain class iv antiarrhythmics and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Adenosine
units.mechanism: Adenosine activates cardiac A1 receptors, reducing cAMP and increasing potassium conductance to briefly suppress AV nodal conduction. Its very short half-life produces transient flushing or chest discomfort and can terminate AV node-dependent reentry.
units.case: A rapidly cleared IV drug briefly blocks AV conduction and terminates a regular narrow-complex reentrant rhythm.
units.pitfall: It is not a universal treatment for all tachycardias; severe bronchospastic disease and particular rhythm contexts require caution.
units.objective: Explain adenosine and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Magnesium and torsades
units.mechanism: Magnesium suppresses triggered activity associated with prolonged repolarization and is used in torsades de pointes even when the measured serum magnesium is not low. Removing provoking causes remains important.
units.case: A patient develops polymorphic VT with prolonged QT, and a drug used for this rhythm works even without documented low serum magnesium.
units.pitfall: Polymorphic VT with normal QT is a different problem and should not automatically be assigned the same mechanism.
units.objective: Explain magnesium and torsades and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Digoxin AV nodal effects
units.mechanism: Beyond increasing intracellular calcium, digoxin enhances vagal influence and slows AV nodal conduction. This can reduce ventricular response in some atrial arrhythmias but also contributes to AV block in toxicity.
units.case: A cardiac glycoside slows the ventricular rate by increasing parasympathetic influence on the AV node.
units.pitfall: Its nodal action can be harmful in pre-excited AF because bypass conduction is not controlled in the same way.
units.objective: Explain digoxin av nodal effects and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Early versus delayed afterdepolarizations
units.mechanism: Early afterdepolarizations occur before full repolarization, often with a prolonged action potential. Delayed afterdepolarizations occur after repolarization and are promoted by intracellular calcium overload, including digoxin toxicity.
units.case: One triggered rhythm follows a long QT during phase 2 or 3, while another follows complete repolarization in calcium-overloaded cells.
units.pitfall: Both are triggered activity, but their timing and precipitating physiology are different.
units.objective: Explain early versus delayed afterdepolarizations and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Staphylococcus aureus endocarditis
units.mechanism: A highly virulent organism can invade previously normal valves and cause rapidly destructive infection. Bacteremia, acute valve dysfunction, abscess formation, and metastatic infection may occur.
units.case: An acutely ill patient develops valve destruction during S. aureus bacteremia despite no known previous valve lesion.
units.pitfall: A normal valve history does not protect against infection by a sufficiently virulent organism.
units.objective: Explain staphylococcus aureus endocarditis and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Viridans streptococcal endocarditis
units.mechanism: Oral streptococci can seed platelet–fibrin deposits on damaged valves during bacteremia. A more indolent course with underlying structural valve disease is a classic association.
units.case: A patient with a previously damaged valve develops subacute fever and blood cultures growing oral flora streptococci.
units.pitfall: A temporal dental history is not required, and routine daily activities can also produce transient bacteremia.
units.objective: Explain viridans streptococcal endocarditis and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Tricuspid injection-associated infection
units.mechanism: Organisms introduced into systemic venous blood first encounter right-sided valves, particularly the tricuspid valve. S. aureus is common, and embolic fragments may travel to the pulmonary circulation.
units.case: A patient who injects drugs has fever, a right-sided regurgitant murmur, and multiple peripheral pulmonary septic emboli.
units.pitfall: Injection-associated infection can also involve left-sided valves; the association is strong but not exclusive.
units.objective: Explain tricuspid injection-associated infection and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Prosthetic valve infection
units.mechanism: Artificial valve surfaces permit microbial adherence and biofilm formation. Coagulase-negative staphylococci are a classic cause, although likely pathogens vary with timing and exposure.
units.case: A patient with an artificial valve develops infection involving organisms able to form a persistent surface biofilm.
units.pitfall: No single organism explains all early or late prosthetic valve infections.
units.objective: Explain prosthetic valve infection and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Enterococcal endocarditis
units.mechanism: Enterococci from gastrointestinal or genitourinary sources can establish valve infection, often in older patients or those with relevant bacteremia risk. Their intrinsic resistance patterns affect antimicrobial choices.
units.case: An older patient develops persistent enterococcal bacteremia with an infected valve after a genitourinary source is identified.
units.pitfall: The source association helps reasoning but does not establish the diagnosis without evidence of endocardial infection.
units.objective: Explain enterococcal endocarditis and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Streptococcus gallolyticus association
units.mechanism: Bacteremia or endocarditis caused by S. gallolyticus is associated with colorectal neoplasia and should prompt consideration of colonic evaluation in clinical care. The association does not mean every infected patient has cancer.
units.case: Blood cultures identify an organism formerly grouped as S. bovis in a patient with endocarditis, raising concern for an occult colorectal lesion.
units.pitfall: Association is not inevitability; the finding is a reason to investigate rather than to assume a malignancy is present.
units.objective: Explain streptococcus gallolyticus association and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: HACEK organisms
units.mechanism: A group of fastidious gram-negative oral organisms can cause subacute endocarditis. Their growth characteristics historically contributed to delayed culture recognition, although modern blood culture systems detect many cases.
units.case: An oral-source fastidious gram-negative organism causes a slowly progressive valve infection.
units.pitfall: Fastidious growth does not mean every case is permanently culture negative.
units.objective: Explain hacek organisms and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Culture-negative endocarditis
units.mechanism: Prior antibiotics or organisms requiring special testing can yield negative routine blood cultures despite endocardial infection. Coxiella and Bartonella are classic considerations in the appropriate exposure setting.
units.case: A patient with valve vegetations and compatible illness has negative routine cultures after receiving antibiotics before sampling.
units.pitfall: A negative culture does not prove a sterile lesion; microbiologic technique and previous treatment affect detection.
units.objective: Explain culture-negative endocarditis and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Infective vegetations
units.mechanism: Platelets, fibrin, inflammatory material, and microorganisms accumulate on endocardial surfaces. Friable vegetations can damage valves and release septic emboli into downstream vascular beds.
units.case: Valve microscopy shows bacteria embedded in a platelet–fibrin mass that sheds infected fragments into the circulation.
units.pitfall: Vegetations also occur in sterile disorders, so morphology and microbiologic context must be integrated.
units.objective: Explain infective vegetations and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Systemic septic embolization
units.mechanism: Left-sided infected vegetations can send emboli to the brain, spleen, kidneys, and other systemic organs. Resulting infarction or infected vascular lesions can produce focal complications.
units.case: A patient with mitral valve infection suddenly develops a focal neurologic deficit and splenic infarction.
units.pitfall: Right-sided vegetations typically embolize to the lungs rather than directly into systemic arterial organs without a shunt.
units.objective: Explain systemic septic embolization and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Janeway lesions
units.mechanism: Painless erythematous lesions on palms or soles are classically associated with septic microembolic phenomena in infective endocarditis. Their presence supports a systemic embolic process.
units.case: A febrile patient with valve infection develops painless red lesions on the soles.
units.pitfall: These lesions are not present in every patient and are not independently diagnostic.
units.objective: Explain janeway lesions and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Osler nodes
units.mechanism: Tender nodules on fingers or toes are classically associated with immune-mediated phenomena in endocarditis, although pathologic mechanisms can overlap. Pain helps distinguish the traditional bedside description from Janeway lesions.
units.case: A patient with endocarditis develops small painful nodules on the pads of the fingers.
units.pitfall: The classic immune-versus-embolic distinction is useful for study but is not perfectly exclusive on pathology.
units.objective: Explain osler nodes and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Immune-complex glomerulonephritis
units.mechanism: Persistent endovascular infection can generate circulating immune complexes that deposit in glomeruli and trigger inflammation. Hematuria, proteinuria, renal dysfunction, and reduced complement may occur.
units.case: A patient with persistent valve infection develops hematuria and low complement from an immune-mediated renal process.
units.pitfall: Renal injury in endocarditis also has other causes, including emboli, hemodynamic injury, and drug effects.
units.objective: Explain immune-complex glomerulonephritis and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Perivalvular abscess
units.mechanism: Extension of endocardial infection into nearby tissue can form an abscess. New conduction abnormalities, especially AV block in aortic valve infection, can signal involvement near the conduction system.
units.case: During aortic valve infection, a patient develops a new PR prolongation and then AV block.
units.pitfall: An ECG change in this context can reflect structural infectious extension rather than merely a medication effect.
units.objective: Explain perivalvular abscess and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Acute rheumatic fever
units.mechanism: An immune response after group A streptococcal pharyngitis can cross-react with host tissues, producing migratory polyarthritis, carditis, chorea, skin findings, and subcutaneous nodules. It is not direct bacterial invasion of the valves.
units.case: Weeks after untreated streptococcal sore throat, a child develops migratory arthritis and carditis.
units.pitfall: The classic trigger is pharyngitis; not every preceding streptococcal infection carries the same established association.
units.objective: Explain acute rheumatic fever and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Aschoff bodies
units.mechanism: Granulomatous inflammatory foci with central fibrinoid change and activated macrophages are characteristic of rheumatic carditis. They reflect immune-mediated myocardial inflammation during the acute disease.
units.case: Myocardial tissue in a child with poststreptococcal carditis contains distinctive inflammatory nodules with central fibrinoid material.
units.pitfall: These foci are a histologic manifestation of rheumatic injury rather than bacterial vegetations.
units.objective: Explain aschoff bodies and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Anitschkow cells
units.mechanism: Activated macrophages in rheumatic inflammatory lesions can show elongated nuclei with centrally wavy chromatin, creating the classic caterpillar appearance. They may be found within Aschoff bodies.
units.case: A macrophage in a rheumatic myocardial lesion has an elongated nucleus with a central ribbon of wavy chromatin.
units.pitfall: A named cellular appearance is an association to interpret within the surrounding tissue pattern.
units.objective: Explain anitschkow cells and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Chronic rheumatic mitral disease
units.mechanism: Repeated or persistent immune-mediated valve injury causes fibrosis, commissural fusion, and chordal thickening. The mitral valve is most often affected, with a classic fish-mouth stenotic opening in advanced disease.
units.case: Years after rheumatic fever, a patient has fused mitral commissures and shortened thickened chordae causing a diastolic inflow obstruction.
units.pitfall: Acute rheumatic valve dysfunction can be regurgitant, whereas chronic scarring commonly creates stenosis.
units.objective: Explain chronic rheumatic mitral disease and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis
units.mechanism: Sterile platelet–fibrin vegetations occur in hypercoagulable states, including advanced malignancy. They can embolize but generally lack the destructive inflammation and microorganisms of infective endocarditis.
units.case: A patient with advanced adenocarcinoma has recurrent arterial emboli and sterile friable valve vegetations.
units.pitfall: Negative cultures alone do not establish this diagnosis; treated or fastidious infection must remain in the differential.
units.objective: Explain nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Libman–Sacks endocarditis
units.mechanism: Systemic lupus erythematosus can produce sterile inflammatory valve lesions on either or both surfaces of leaflets and other endocardial sites. The mechanism is immune-mediated rather than direct bacterial infection.
units.case: A patient with lupus has sterile vegetations involving both sides of mitral leaflets.
units.pitfall: The characteristic distribution is helpful, but lupus does not prevent a patient from also developing true infective endocarditis.
units.objective: Explain libman–sacks endocarditis and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Cardiogenic shock profile
units.mechanism: Pump failure reduces cardiac output and usually provokes compensatory elevation of systemic resistance. LV failure commonly raises PCWP, distinguishing its filling-pressure pattern from volume depletion.
units.case: After a large LV infarct, measured CO is low, SVR is high, and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is high.
units.pitfall: An isolated RV problem can have a different left-sided filling-pressure pattern despite a cardiac cause of shock.
units.objective: Explain cardiogenic shock profile and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Hypovolemic shock profile
units.mechanism: Loss of intravascular volume reduces venous return, preload, and cardiac output. Sympathetic compensation increases heart rate and systemic resistance while right- and left-sided filling pressures fall.
units.case: A patient with major blood loss has low CO, low PCWP, tachycardia, and high SVR.
units.pitfall: A normal early hemoglobin concentration does not exclude acute hemorrhage before redistribution occurs.
units.objective: Explain hypovolemic shock profile and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Early septic shock profile
units.mechanism: Inflammatory mediators produce vasodilation, endothelial dysfunction, and altered microcirculatory flow. Early hyperdynamic shock can show low SVR and high CO despite inadequate effective tissue oxygen delivery.
units.case: A febrile patient with infection has warm extremities, low systemic resistance, and elevated measured cardiac output.
units.pitfall: Septic shock can later include myocardial depression and low output; the high-output pattern is not universal.
units.objective: Explain early septic shock profile and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Anaphylactic shock
units.mechanism: Systemic mediator release causes vasodilation and increased vascular permeability, often with bronchospasm. Reduced effective circulating volume and low SVR produce distributive shock.
units.case: Minutes after an allergen exposure, a patient develops hypotension, wheezing, urticaria, and rapidly worsening vascular leak.
units.pitfall: Skin findings can be absent, so their absence does not reliably exclude severe anaphylaxis.
units.objective: Explain anaphylactic shock and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Neurogenic shock
units.mechanism: Loss of sympathetic vascular tone after high spinal injury causes vasodilation and relative or absolute bradycardia rather than the usual compensatory tachycardia. Reduced venous return contributes to low output.
units.case: After a cervical spinal injury, a hypotensive patient has warm skin and an inappropriately slow heart rate.
units.pitfall: Other causes of hypotension, especially hemorrhage in trauma, must still be assessed.
units.objective: Explain neurogenic shock and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Massive pulmonary embolism
units.mechanism: Acute obstruction of the pulmonary arterial bed sharply increases RV afterload, impairs RV output, and reduces LV preload. Obstructive shock may occur with elevated right-sided pressure and relatively low left-sided filling.
units.case: A patient develops abrupt dyspnea, shock, RV dilation, and high pulmonary vascular resistance without primary LV pump failure.
units.pitfall: A normal or nonspecific ECG does not exclude a dangerous pulmonary vascular obstruction.
units.objective: Explain massive pulmonary embolism and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Tension pneumothorax
units.mechanism: Progressively elevated intrapleural pressure compresses intrathoracic veins and impairs venous return, causing obstructive shock. Ventilation is also compromised, with asymmetric breath sounds and pressure-related collapse.
units.case: After chest trauma, a patient becomes hypotensive with severe respiratory distress, unilateral absent breath sounds, and distended neck veins.
units.pitfall: Tracheal deviation is a late and inconsistent sign; the physiology is not dependent on seeing it.
units.objective: Explain tension pneumothorax and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Tamponade shock integration
units.mechanism: A pressurized pericardial space restricts diastolic filling and reduces forward output. Venous pressure rises despite inadequate ventricular filling, producing an obstructive rather than primary contractile failure pattern.
units.case: Hypotension with raised JVP follows rapid accumulation of fluid around a heart that cannot expand during diastole.
units.pitfall: High venous pressure does not always mean the ventricle has an adequate usable preload volume.
units.objective: Explain tamponade shock integration and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Lactate interpretation
units.mechanism: Elevated lactate can reflect impaired oxygen delivery, accelerated adrenergic glycolysis, reduced clearance, or combinations. It supports assessment of severe illness but does not uniquely identify one type of shock.
units.case: A patient with sepsis has increased lactate from both impaired perfusion and increased adrenergic metabolic activity.
units.pitfall: Lactate is not a direct one-to-one measure of tissue hypoxia and must be interpreted over time and in context.
units.objective: Explain lactate interpretation and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Mixed venous oxygen saturation
units.mechanism: Mixed venous saturation reflects the balance between systemic oxygen delivery and consumption. Low CO often increases extraction and lowers SvO2, whereas sepsis can produce high values when extraction or flow distribution is impaired.
units.case: A low-output patient has a low pulmonary arterial oxygen saturation because tissues extract a larger fraction of delivered oxygen.
units.pitfall: A high value does not guarantee adequate cellular oxygen use, particularly in distributive states.
units.objective: Explain mixed venous oxygen saturation and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure
units.mechanism: Balloon occlusion in a suitable pulmonary arterial branch estimates downstream pulmonary venous and left atrial pressure under appropriate conditions. It is often used as a surrogate for LV filling pressure.
units.case: A catheter's wedged pressure rises with left atrial hypertension from LV failure or mitral obstruction.
units.pitfall: Mitral disease, alveolar pressure, and measurement conditions can prevent wedge pressure from directly representing LV end-diastolic pressure.
units.objective: Explain pulmonary capillary wedge pressure and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Oxygen delivery equation
units.mechanism: Systemic oxygen delivery equals cardiac output multiplied by arterial oxygen content, with unit conversion as needed. A defect in hemoglobin, saturation, or flow can reduce delivery even if the other components are normal.
units.case: A patient with normal oxygen saturation has reduced tissue oxygen delivery because both hemoglobin concentration and cardiac output are low.
units.pitfall: Supplemental oxygen cannot fully correct low delivery due to severe anemia or very low flow when saturation is already high.
units.objective: Explain oxygen delivery equation and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Arteriovenous fistula hemodynamics
units.mechanism: A low-resistance connection bypassing arterioles lowers systemic resistance and increases venous return. Cardiac output rises to maintain arterial pressure, potentially causing high-output failure when the shunt is large.
units.case: After creation of a large dialysis access, a patient develops a high-flow circulatory state and increased cardiac workload.
units.pitfall: The increased output is compensatory and does not necessarily indicate unusually healthy myocardial performance.
units.objective: Explain arteriovenous fistula hemodynamics and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Hemorrhage compensation
units.mechanism: Arterial baroreflex activation increases sympathetic tone, producing tachycardia, arteriolar constriction, and venoconstriction. RAAS and vasopressin support volume and pressure over longer intervals.
units.case: Immediately after blood loss, a patient's skin becomes cool and pulse rapid before hormonal volume retention can restore circulating volume.
units.pitfall: The absence of tachycardia can occur with drugs, age, or autonomic factors and does not rule out significant blood loss.
units.objective: Explain hemorrhage compensation and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Fluid responsiveness
units.mechanism: A rise in stroke volume after a reversible increase in preload suggests that the ventricle is operating on the ascending portion of its function curve. Responsiveness is a physiologic observation, not an automatic indication to give more fluid.
units.case: A passive leg raise transiently increases stroke volume, indicating the circulation can augment output when venous return increases.
units.pitfall: A patient can be fluid responsive yet still be harmed by fluid because of pulmonary edema or other constraints.
units.objective: Explain fluid responsiveness and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Norepinephrine receptor physiology
units.mechanism: Predominant α1-mediated vasoconstriction raises systemic resistance and pressure, while β1 activity can support contractility. The final heart-rate response reflects direct cardiac effects and reflex responses to pressure elevation.
units.case: A vasoactive infusion raises SVR and arterial pressure through α1 stimulation while providing some β1 inotropic activity.
units.pitfall: Receptor selectivity is relative and dose-dependent; a single label does not predict every hemodynamic response.
units.objective: Explain norepinephrine receptor physiology and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Dobutamine receptor physiology
units.mechanism: Predominant β1 stimulation increases contractility and cardiac output, with β2-related vasodilation contributing to reduced resistance in some settings. Increased myocardial oxygen demand and tachyarrhythmia are potential consequences.
units.case: An inotropic infusion improves forward flow mainly by increasing ventricular contractile force rather than by raising systemic resistance.
units.pitfall: Raising output does not necessarily raise pressure when systemic vasodilation accompanies the inotropic effect.
units.objective: Explain dobutamine receptor physiology and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Right ventricular infarct physiology
units.mechanism: An infarcted RV cannot effectively deliver blood to the left heart, reducing LV preload. Hypotension, elevated JVP, and relatively clear lungs after inferior MI are classic clues.
units.case: After inferior infarction, a patient has hypotension and distended neck veins without pulmonary edema, with ST elevation in right-sided leads.
units.pitfall: Preload reduction may worsen output in this setting, and the presentation differs from congested LV pump failure.
units.objective: Explain right ventricular infarct physiology and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Tissue hypoxia categories
units.mechanism: Hypoxemic hypoxia reduces arterial oxygenation, anemic hypoxia reduces hemoglobin capacity, ischemic hypoxia reduces flow, and histotoxic hypoxia impairs cellular utilization. PaO2 can be normal in several nonhypoxemic forms.
units.case: A cyanide-exposed patient has adequate arterial oxygen tension but impaired cellular oxygen use and abnormally high venous oxygen content.
units.pitfall: Normal PaO2 only addresses dissolved oxygen tension; it does not prove normal transport or utilization.
units.objective: Explain tissue hypoxia categories and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

units.title: Carbon monoxide oxygen transport
units.mechanism: Carbon monoxide reduces available hemoglobin binding sites and increases oxygen affinity at remaining sites, impairing unloading. PaO2 can remain normal, and standard pulse oximetry may be misleading; co-oximetry measures dyshemoglobins.
units.case: After smoke exposure, a patient has headache and tissue hypoxia despite normal arterial oxygen tension and a reassuring conventional pulse oximeter reading.
units.pitfall: A normal PaO2 does not detect impaired hemoglobin binding, and a normal conventional saturation reading does not exclude carbon monoxide toxicity.
units.objective: Explain carbon monoxide oxygen transport and distinguish its mechanism from related cardiovascular concepts.

questions.q: A patient has a heart rate of 75/min, EDV of 120 mL, and ESV of 50 mL. The calculated flow from the left ventricle is 5.25 L/min. Which concept is best illustrated?

questions.why: Increased end-diastolic fiber length increases force generation within the physiologic range through length-dependent activation. questions.why: Preload describes myocardial fiber stretch before contraction and is often approximated by end-diastolic volume. A filling pressure should not be treated as interchangeable with ventricular volume when compliance differs.

This option describes dynamic exercise response: During dynamic exercise, sympathetic drive increases heart rate and contractility while local metabolites dilate vessels in active muscle. Cardiac output rises and total systemic resistance usually falls; systolic pressure rises more than diastolic pressure. The target concept is preload. Its defining case is: Two ventricles have the same end-diastolic volume but different filling pressures because one has a stiffer wall.

questions.q: Tachycardia and elevated LV filling pressure reduce the time and pressure gradient available to perfuse the left ventricular subendocardium. Which concept is best illustrated?

Baroreceptor reflex
Mean arterial pressure
Contractility
questions.why: Left ventricular contraction compresses intramyocardial vessels, limiting left coronary flow during systole. Most LV perfusion occurs during diastole, with driving pressure approximated by aortic diastolic pressure minus LV end-diastolic pressure. The right ventricle has lower systolic pressure, so right coronary flow is less restricted to diastole.
rationales: Left ventricular contraction compresses intramyocardial vessels, limiting left coronary flow during systole. Most LV perfusion occurs during diastole, with driving pressure approximated by aortic diastolic pressure minus LV end-diastolic pressure. This option describes baroreceptor reflex: Carotid sinus and aortic arch stretch receptors signal through cranial nerves IX and X. Falling arterial pressure reduces firing, increases sympathetic output, and decreases vagal tone, raising heart rate and vascular tone. The target concept is coronary perfusion timing. Its defining case is: Tachycardia and elevated LV filling pressure reduce the time and pressure gradient available to perfuse the left ventricular subendocardium.

This option describes mean arterial pressure: At ordinary heart rates, MAP is approximately diastolic pressure plus one third of pulse pressure. Its defining case is: Tachycardia and elevated LV filling pressure reduce the time and pressure gradient available to perfuse the left ventricular subendocardium.

This option describes contractility: Increased inotropy raises force generation at a given preload and afterload. It steepens the end-systolic pressure–volume relationship, reduces ESV, and increases stroke volume and ejection fraction. The target concept is coronary perfusion timing. Its defining case is: Tachycardia and elevated LV filling pressure reduce the time and pressure gradient available to perfuse the left ventricular subendocardium.

questions.q: A patient with severe anemia has a normal PaO2 and oxygen saturation but reduced oxygen carried per unit of blood. Which concept is best illustrated?

Preload
Pressure–volume loop phases
Myocardial oxygen demand
questions.why: Arterial oxygen content is approximately 1.34 times hemoglobin times fractional saturation plus 0.003 times PaO2, in mL O2/dL. Hemoglobin-bound oxygen accounts for most content under ordinary conditions. Normal saturation does not establish normal oxygen content when hemoglobin concentration is low.

Hemoglobin-bound oxygen accounts for most content under ordinary conditions. This option describes preload: Preload describes myocardial fiber stretch before contraction and is often approximated by end-diastolic volume. Filling pressure is only an indirect surrogate because compliance affects the pressure–volume relationship. The target concept is oxygen content. Its defining case is: A patient with severe anemia has a normal PaO2 and oxygen saturation but reduced oxygen carried per unit of blood.

This option describes pressure–volume loop phases: Isovolumetric contraction begins after AV valve closure and precedes semilunar valve opening. Isovolumetric relaxation begins after semilunar closure; volume is unchanged while pressure falls because all valves are closed. The target concept is oxygen content. Its defining case is: A patient with severe anemia has a normal PaO2 and oxygen saturation but reduced oxygen carried per unit of blood.

questions.q: On standing abruptly, reduced arterial stretch triggers tachycardia and arteriolar constriction within seconds. Which concept is best illustrated?

Afterload
Stroke work
Laplace wall stress

Falling arterial pressure reduces firing, increases sympathetic output, and decreases vagal tone, raising heart rate and vascular tone. Baroreceptors respond rapidly but reset during sustained hypertension; they are not the sole controllers of long-term pressure.

This option describes afterload: Afterload is the load opposing ventricular ejection and relates to arterial pressure, outflow impedance, and wall stress. An acute increase at fixed preload and contractility increases ESV and decreases stroke volume. The target concept is baroreceptor reflex.
