questions.q: A drug slows the upstroke of the ventricular action potential and prolongs ventricular conduction on the surface ECG. Which concept is best illustrated?
a: Ventricular phase 0
PR interval
Mobitz type I block
Atrial flutter
questions.why: Rapid depolarization in working ventricular myocytes is mediated by fast voltage-gated sodium channels. Sodium-channel blockade slows conduction in this tissue and can widen the QRS complex. Nodal tissue uses a calcium-dependent upstroke; the same phase number does not imply the same ion in every cell type.
rationales: Rapid depolarization in working ventricular myocytes is mediated by fast voltage-gated sodium channels. Sodium-channel blockade slows conduction in this tissue and can widen the QRS complex. In this case: A drug slows the upstroke of the ventricular action potential and prolongs ventricular conduction on the surface ECG.

This option describes pr interval: The PR interval extends from onset of atrial depolarization to onset of ventricular depolarization and includes AV nodal delay. A consistently prolonged interval above 200 ms with every P conducted indicates first-degree AV block. The target concept is ventricular phase 0. Its defining case is: A drug slows the upstroke of the ventricular action potential and prolongs ventricular conduction on the surface ECG.

This option describes mobitz type i block: Wenckebach block typically occurs in the AV node and shows progressive PR lengthening followed by a nonconducted P wave. The cycle then repeats, often with grouped beating. The target concept is ventricular phase 0. Its defining case is: A drug slows the upstroke of the ventricular action potential and prolongs ventricular conduction on the surface ECG.

This option describes atrial flutter: A macroreentrant atrial circuit produces organized rapid atrial activity, often with sawtooth flutter waves. AV conduction ratios such as 2:1 can generate a ventricular rate near 150/min when atrial rate is near 300/min. The target concept is ventricular phase 0. Its defining case is: A drug slows the upstroke of the ventricular action potential and prolongs ventricular conduction on the surface ECG.
questions.takeaway: Nodal tissue uses a calcium-dependent upstroke; the same phase number does not imply the same ion in every cell type.

Ventricular repolarization
Muscarinic M2 signaling
First-degree AV block
questions.why: A macroreentrant atrial circuit produces organized rapid atrial activity, often with sawtooth flutter waves. AV conduction ratios such as 2:1 can generate a ventricular rate near 150/min when atrial rate is near 300/min. A ventricular rate near 150 is a clue, not proof; atrial activity and conduction relationships establish the diagnosis.
rationales: A macroreentrant atrial circuit produces organized rapid atrial activity, often with sawtooth flutter waves. AV conduction ratios such as 2:1 can generate a ventricular rate near 150/min when atrial rate is near 300/min. In this case: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia near 150/min is accompanied by repetitive sawtooth atrial deflections, particularly in inferior leads.

This option describes ventricular repolarization: Phase 3 of the ventricular action potential is produced mainly by outward potassium currents as calcium current declines. Delayed repolarization lengthens the action potential and can increase the QT interval. The target concept is atrial flutter. Its defining case is: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia near 150/min is accompanied by repetitive sawtooth atrial deflections, particularly in inferior leads.

This option describes muscarinic m2 signaling: Cardiac M2 receptors couple to Gi, reduce cAMP, and increase potassium conductance in nodal cells. Vagal stimulation slows SA discharge and AV conduction, with less direct effect on ventricular contractility. The target concept is atrial flutter. Its defining case is: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia near 150/min is accompanied by repetitive sawtooth atrial deflections, particularly in inferior leads.

This option describes first-degree av block: All atrial impulses conduct to the ventricles, but AV conduction is delayed, producing a prolonged constant PR interval. No QRS complexes are dropped because of block in this pattern. The target concept is atrial flutter. Its defining case is: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia near 150/min is accompanied by repetitive sawtooth atrial deflections, particularly in inferior leads.
questions.takeaway: A ventricular rate near 150 is a clue, not proof; atrial activity and conduction relationships establish the diagnosis.

questions.q: A patient has abrupt onset and offset of a regular narrow-complex tachycardia that terminates when AV nodal conduction is transiently blocked. Which concept is best illustrated?
a: AV nodal reentry
Nodal phase 0
PR interval
Mobitz type I block
questions.why: Dual AV nodal pathways with differing conduction and refractory properties can sustain a reentrant loop. The resulting tachycardia is commonly regular and narrow, with atrial activation hidden in or immediately after the QRS. Not every supraventricular tachycardia is AV nodal reentry; accessory-pathway-mediated reentry can behave similarly.
rationales: Dual AV nodal pathways with differing conduction and refractory properties can sustain a reentrant loop. The resulting tachycardia is commonly regular and narrow, with atrial activation hidden in or immediately after the QRS. In this case: A patient has abrupt onset and offset of a regular narrow-complex tachycardia that terminates when AV nodal conduction is transiently blocked.

This option describes nodal phase 0: The upstroke in SA and AV nodal cells depends mainly on L-type calcium channels. Non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers slow AV nodal conduction and may prolong the PR interval. The target concept is av nodal reentry. Its defining case is: A patient has abrupt onset and offset of a regular narrow-complex tachycardia that terminates when AV nodal conduction is transiently blocked.

This option describes pr interval: The PR interval extends from onset of atrial depolarization to onset of ventricular depolarization and includes AV nodal delay. A consistently prolonged interval above 200 ms with every P conducted indicates first-degree AV block. The target concept is av nodal reentry. Its defining case is: A patient has abrupt onset and offset of a regular narrow-complex tachycardia that terminates when AV nodal conduction is transiently blocked.

This option describes mobitz type i block: Wenckebach block typically occurs in the AV node and shows progressive PR lengthening followed by a nonconducted P wave. The cycle then repeats, often with grouped beating. The target concept is av nodal reentry. Its defining case is: A patient has abrupt onset and offset of a regular narrow-complex tachycardia that terminates when AV nodal conduction is transiently blocked.
questions.takeaway: Not every supraventricular tachycardia is AV nodal reentry; accessory-pathway-mediated reentry can behave similarly.

questions.q: A baseline ECG shows a slurred initial QRS upstroke and short PR before episodes of rapid palpitations. Which concept is best illustrated?
a: Wolff–Parkinson–White pattern
Funny current
QRS complex
Mobitz type II block
questions.why: An accessory AV pathway can bypass normal AV nodal delay, causing a short PR interval, delta wave, and widened QRS in sinus rhythm. It can also participate in reentrant tachycardia. AV nodal blockers can be dangerous in pre-excited atrial fibrillation because conduction through the accessory pathway may accelerate.
rationales: An accessory AV pathway can bypass normal AV nodal delay, causing a short PR interval, delta wave, and widened QRS in sinus rhythm. It can also participate in reentrant tachycardia. In this case: A baseline ECG shows a slurred initial QRS upstroke and short PR before episodes of rapid palpitations.

This option describes funny current: Hyperpolarization-activated HCN channels carry the mixed inward funny current contributing to spontaneous phase 4 depolarization. cAMP increases pacemaker activity; ivabradine reduces sinus rate by inhibiting this current. The target concept is wolff–parkinson–white pattern. Its defining case is: A baseline ECG shows a slurred initial QRS upstroke and short PR before episodes of rapid palpitations.

This option describes qrs complex: The QRS represents ventricular depolarization. Widening can result from bundle-branch block, ventricular origin of activation, sodium-channel blockade, or metabolic conduction disturbance such as severe hyperkalemia. The target concept is wolff–parkinson–white pattern. Its defining case is: A baseline ECG shows a slurred initial QRS upstroke and short PR before episodes of rapid palpitations.

This option describes mobitz type ii block: Intermittent atrial impulses fail to conduct despite a stable PR interval in conducted beats, often indicating His–Purkinje disease. The pattern can progress to complete AV block. The target concept is wolff–parkinson–white pattern. Its defining case is: A baseline ECG shows a slurred initial QRS upstroke and short PR before episodes of rapid palpitations.
questions.takeaway: AV nodal blockers can be dangerous in pre-excited atrial fibrillation because conduction through the accessory pathway may accelerate.

questions.q: A patient with renal failure develops tall peaked T waves followed by widening QRS complexes as potassium rises. Which concept is best illustrated?
a: Hyperkalemic ECG progression
Beta-1 signaling
QT interval
Third-degree AV block
questions.why: Rising extracellular potassium can produce peaked T waves, PR prolongation, P-wave loss, and QRS widening, potentially progressing to a sine-wave pattern. Severe hyperkalemia destabilizes conduction and requires urgent assessment. ECG findings are variable and cannot reliably exclude dangerous hyperkalemia when absent.
rationales: Rising extracellular potassium can produce peaked T waves, PR prolongation, P-wave loss, and QRS widening, potentially progressing to a sine-wave pattern. Severe hyperkalemia destabilizes conduction and requires urgent assessment. In this case: A patient with renal failure develops tall peaked T waves followed by widening QRS complexes as potassium rises.

This option describes beta-1 signaling: β1 receptor stimulation activates Gs, adenylyl cyclase, cAMP, and protein kinase A. Increased calcium handling enhances contractility, while nodal effects increase pacemaker rate and AV conduction. The target concept is hyperkalemic ecg progression. Its defining case is: A patient with renal failure develops tall peaked T waves followed by widening QRS complexes as potassium rises.

This option describes qt interval: The QT spans ventricular depolarization and repolarization and varies with heart rate. QT correction estimates rate-adjusted duration; prolonged repolarization predisposes to early afterdepolarizations and torsades de pointes. The target concept is hyperkalemic ecg progression. Its defining case is: A patient with renal failure develops tall peaked T waves followed by widening QRS complexes as potassium rises.

This option describes third-degree av block: Complete interruption of atrial-to-ventricular conduction produces independent atrial and ventricular rhythms. An escape focus maintains ventricular activation, and the PR relationship varies without organized conduction. The target concept is hyperkalemic ecg progression. Its defining case is: A patient with renal failure develops tall peaked T waves followed by widening QRS complexes as potassium rises.
questions.takeaway: ECG findings are variable and cannot reliably exclude dangerous hyperkalemia when absent.

questions.q: After starting a QT-prolonging drug, a patient develops pause-associated polymorphic VT with complexes appearing to twist around the baseline. Which concept is best illustrated?
a: Torsades de pointes
Muscarinic M2 signaling
First-degree AV block
Atrial fibrillation
questions.why: This polymorphic ventricular tachycardia occurs in the setting of prolonged repolarization and often follows early afterdepolarizations. Drug effects, low potassium, low magnesium, and congenital long-QT syndromes are important settings. Polymorphic VT with a normal QT may have another mechanism, including acute ischemia.

Drug effects, low potassium, low magnesium, and congenital long-QT syndromes are important settings. Vagal stimulation slows SA discharge and AV conduction, with less direct effect on ventricular contractility. The target concept is torsades de pointes. Its defining case is: After starting a QT-prolonging drug, a patient develops pause-associated polymorphic VT with complexes appearing to twist around the baseline.

This option describes first-degree av block: All atrial impulses conduct to the ventricles, but AV conduction is delayed, producing a prolonged constant PR interval. No QRS complexes are dropped because of block in this pattern. The target concept is torsades de pointes. Its defining case is: After starting a QT-prolonging drug, a patient develops pause-associated polymorphic VT with complexes appearing to twist around the baseline.

questions.q: A patient develops predictable substernal pressure while climbing stairs that resolves after several minutes of rest, without evidence of acute myocardial injury. Which concept is best illustrated?
a: Stable angina
Circumflex lateral territory
Early infarct histology
Papillary muscle rupture
questions.why: A fixed coronary atherosclerotic narrowing limits flow reserve, creating demand-induced ischemia without acute myocardial necrosis. Symptoms are reproducible with exertion and improve when demand falls. Relief with nitroglycerin is not specific enough to diagnose coronary ischemia on its own.
rationales: A fixed coronary atherosclerotic narrowing limits flow reserve, creating demand-induced ischemia without acute myocardial necrosis. Symptoms are reproducible with exertion and improve when demand falls. In this case: A patient develops predictable substernal pressure while climbing stairs that resolves after several minutes of rest, without evidence of acute myocardial injury.

This option describes circumflex lateral territory: The left circumflex artery supplies portions of the lateral LV through obtuse marginal branches. Ischemia can affect lateral leads such as I, aVL, V5, and V6 depending on branch anatomy. The target concept is stable angina. Its defining case is: A patient develops predictable substernal pressure while climbing stairs that resolves after several minutes of rest, without evidence of acute myocardial injury.

This option describes early infarct histology: Coagulative necrosis evolves during the first day after ischemic cell death, with hypereosinophilic myocytes and loss of nuclei. Neutrophils accumulate over the following early days as acute inflammation develops. The target concept is stable angina. Its defining case is: A patient develops predictable substernal pressure while climbing stairs that resolves after several minutes of rest, without evidence of acute myocardial injury.

This option describes papillary muscle rupture: Ischemic rupture of a papillary muscle causes acute severe mitral regurgitation, pulmonary edema, and possible shock. The posteromedial muscle is vulnerable because it typically has a single arterial supply through the PDA. The target concept is stable angina. Its defining case is: A patient develops predictable substernal pressure while climbing stairs that resolves after several minutes of rest, without evidence of acute myocardial injury.
questions.takeaway: Relief with nitroglycerin is not specific enough to diagnose coronary ischemia on its own.

questions.q: A previously noncritical coronary plaque with a thin fibrous cap develops surface disruption and an acute superimposed thrombus. Which concept is best illustrated?
a: Plaque rupture
Coronary dominance
Macrophage clearance
True ventricular aneurysm
questions.why: Disruption of a vulnerable fibrous cap exposes thrombogenic material and activates platelets and coagulation. Acute thrombus formation can rapidly reduce coronary perfusion even when the preexisting narrowing was not severe. Plaque instability, not just percent stenosis, contributes to acute coronary syndromes.
rationales: Disruption of a vulnerable fibrous cap exposes thrombogenic material and activates platelets and coagulation. Acute thrombus formation can rapidly reduce coronary perfusion even when the preexisting narrowing was not severe. In this case: A previously noncritical coronary plaque with a thin fibrous cap develops surface disruption and an acute superimposed thrombus.

This option describes coronary dominance: Dominance is defined by the artery that gives rise to the posterior descending artery, rather than by the artery with the largest lumen or total flow. Right dominance is most common. The target concept is plaque rupture. Its defining case is: A previously noncritical coronary plaque with a thin fibrous cap develops surface disruption and an acute superimposed thrombus.

This option describes macrophage clearance: Around days 3–7 after infarction, macrophages clear dead myocardium before strong collagen replacement is established. The mechanically weakened tissue is vulnerable to rupture. The target concept is plaque rupture. Its defining case is: A previously noncritical coronary plaque with a thin fibrous cap develops surface disruption and an acute superimposed thrombus.

This option describes true ventricular aneurysm: A healed transmural infarct can form a broad-based dyskinetic outpouching containing scarred ventricular wall. It can cause mural thrombus, arrhythmia, and persistent ST elevation but is less rupture-prone than a pseudoaneurysm. The target concept is plaque rupture. Its defining case is: A previously noncritical coronary plaque with a thin fibrous cap develops surface disruption and an acute superimposed thrombus.
questions.takeaway: Plaque instability, not just percent stenosis, contributes to acute coronary syndromes.

This option describes s3 gallop: Rapid early diastolic filling can generate an S3 when blood enters a dilated or volume-overloaded ventricle. questions.q: A young adult has right ventricular enlargement and fixed splitting of S2 with a pulmonary flow murmur. Which concept is best illustrated?

Persistent truncus arteriosus
Atrioventricular septal defect
Endocardial cushion development

The lesion is strongly associated with trisomy 21. The target concept is secundum atrial septal defect. Its defining case is: A young adult has right ventricular enlargement and fixed splitting of S2 with a pulmonary flow murmur.

This option describes endocardial cushion development: Cushions help form the atrioventricular septal complex and portions of the AV valves. Abnormal development produces characteristic inlet septal and valve abnormalities. The target concept is secundum atrial septal defect. Its defining case is: A young adult has right ventricular enlargement and fixed splitting of S2 with a pulmonary flow murmur.

questions.q: An otherwise structurally normal atrial septum has unfused overlapping flaps that can open when right atrial pressure temporarily exceeds left atrial pressure. Which concept is best illustrated?
a: Patent foramen ovale
Tricuspid atresia
Ebstein anomaly
Fetal circulatory shunts
questions.why: Failure of postnatal fusion between septal flaps leaves a potential atrial passage without a true deficiency of septal tissue. Transient right-to-left pressure gradients can permit paradoxical embolism. This common finding is anatomically different from a true atrial septal tissue defect.

This option describes tricuspid atresia: Absence of a patent right atrioventricular connection prevents direct RA-to-RV flow, often leaving a hypoplastic RV. An atrial communication is required for systemic venous blood to leave the right atrium. The target concept is patent foramen ovale. Its defining case is: An otherwise structurally normal atrial septum has unfused overlapping flaps that can open when right atrial pressure temporarily exceeds left atrial pressure.

This option describes ebstein anomaly: Apical displacement of tricuspid leaflets leads to atrialization of part of the RV and tricuspid regurgitation. Associated atrial shunting and accessory pathways may contribute to cyanosis or arrhythmia. The target concept is patent foramen ovale. Its defining case is: An otherwise structurally normal atrial septum has unfused overlapping flaps that can open when right atrial pressure temporarily exceeds left atrial pressure.

This option describes fetal circulatory shunts: The ductus venosus bypasses much of the liver, the foramen ovale directs RA-to-LA flow, and the ductus arteriosus carries pulmonary arterial blood toward the aorta. questions.q: A premature infant has bounding pulses and a continuous murmur from flow between the aorta and pulmonary artery. Which concept is best illustrated?
a: Patent ductus arteriosus
Total anomalous pulmonary venous return
Hypoplastic left heart syndrome
Postnatal circulation transition
questions.why: Persistence of the fetal aorta-to-pulmonary connection usually causes left-to-right flow after birth, producing continuous flow and a machinery murmur. Prematurity and congenital rubella are classic associations. In duct-dependent congenital lesions, maintaining the connection can be lifesaving rather than something to reverse immediately.
rationales: Persistence of the fetal aorta-to-pulmonary connection usually causes left-to-right flow after birth, producing continuous flow and a machinery murmur. Prematurity and congenital rubella are classic associations. In this case: A premature infant has bounding pulses and a continuous murmur from flow between the aorta and pulmonary artery.

This option describes total anomalous pulmonary venous return: Pulmonary veins connect to systemic venous structures instead of the left atrium. An atrial communication is required for blood to reach the left heart; venous obstruction can cause severe neonatal distress. The target concept is patent ductus arteriosus. Its defining case is: A premature infant has bounding pulses and a continuous murmur from flow between the aorta and pulmonary artery.

This option describes hypoplastic left heart syndrome: Severe underdevelopment of left-sided chambers and outflow structures prevents adequate independent systemic output. Systemic perfusion depends on flow from the pulmonary artery through a patent ductus. The target concept is patent ductus arteriosus. Its defining case is: A premature infant has bounding pulses and a continuous murmur from flow between the aorta and pulmonary artery.

This option describes postnatal circulation transition: Lung expansion lowers pulmonary vascular resistance while cord clamping increases systemic resistance. Increased pulmonary venous return raises LA pressure relative to RA pressure, functionally closing the foramen ovale. The target concept is patent ductus arteriosus. Its defining case is: A premature infant has bounding pulses and a continuous murmur from flow between the aorta and pulmonary artery.
questions.takeaway: In duct-dependent congenital lesions, maintaining the connection can be lifesaving rather than something to reverse immediately.

questions.q: After a large LV infarct, measured CO is low, SVR is high, and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is high. Which concept is best illustrated?
a: Cardiogenic shock profile
Tamponade shock integration
Oxygen delivery equation
Norepinephrine receptor physiology
questions.why: Pump failure reduces cardiac output and usually provokes compensatory elevation of systemic resistance. LV failure commonly raises PCWP, distinguishing its filling-pressure pattern from volume depletion. An isolated RV problem can have a different left-sided filling-pressure pattern despite a cardiac cause of shock.
rationales: Pump failure reduces cardiac output and usually provokes compensatory elevation of systemic resistance. LV failure commonly raises PCWP, distinguishing its filling-pressure pattern from volume depletion. In this case: After a large LV infarct, measured CO is low, SVR is high, and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is high.

This option describes tamponade shock integration: A pressurized pericardial space restricts diastolic filling and reduces forward output. Venous pressure rises despite inadequate ventricular filling, producing an obstructive rather than primary contractile failure pattern. The target concept is cardiogenic shock profile. Its defining case is: After a large LV infarct, measured CO is low, SVR is high, and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is high.

This option describes oxygen delivery equation: Systemic oxygen delivery equals cardiac output multiplied by arterial oxygen content, with unit conversion as needed. A defect in hemoglobin, saturation, or flow can reduce delivery even if the other components are normal. The target concept is cardiogenic shock profile. Its defining case is: After a large LV infarct, measured CO is low, SVR is high, and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is high.

This option describes norepinephrine receptor physiology: Predominant α1-mediated vasoconstriction raises systemic resistance and pressure, while β1 activity can support contractility. The final heart-rate response reflects direct cardiac effects and reflex responses to pressure elevation. The target concept is cardiogenic shock profile. Its defining case is: After a large LV infarct, measured CO is low, SVR is high, and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is high.
questions.takeaway: An isolated RV problem can have a different left-sided filling-pressure pattern despite a cardiac cause of shock.

questions.q: A patient with major blood loss has low CO, low PCWP, tachycardia, and high SVR. Which concept is best illustrated?
a: Hypovolemic shock profile
Lactate interpretation
Arteriovenous fistula hemodynamics
Dobutamine receptor physiology
questions.why: Loss of intravascular volume reduces venous return, preload, and cardiac output. Sympathetic compensation increases heart rate and systemic resistance while right- and left-sided filling pressures fall. A normal early hemoglobin concentration does not exclude acute hemorrhage before redistribution occurs.
rationales: Loss of intravascular volume reduces venous return, preload, and cardiac output. Sympathetic compensation increases heart rate and systemic resistance while right- and left-sided filling pressures fall. In this case: A patient with major blood loss has low CO, low PCWP, tachycardia, and high SVR.

This option describes lactate interpretation: Elevated lactate can reflect impaired oxygen delivery, accelerated adrenergic glycolysis, reduced clearance, or combinations. It supports assessment of severe illness but does not uniquely identify one type of shock. The target concept is hypovolemic shock profile. Its defining case is: A patient with major blood loss has low CO, low PCWP, tachycardia, and high SVR.

This option describes arteriovenous fistula hemodynamics: A low-resistance connection bypassing arterioles lowers systemic resistance and increases venous return. Cardiac output rises to maintain arterial pressure, potentially causing high-output failure when the shunt is large. The target concept is hypovolemic shock profile. Its defining case is: A patient with major blood loss has low CO, low PCWP, tachycardia, and high SVR.

This option describes dobutamine receptor physiology: Predominant β1 stimulation increases contractility and cardiac output, with β2-related vasodilation contributing to reduced resistance in some settings. Increased myocardial oxygen demand and tachyarrhythmia are potential consequences. The target concept is hypovolemic shock profile. Its defining case is: A patient with major blood loss has low CO, low PCWP, tachycardia, and high SVR.
questions.takeaway: A normal early hemoglobin concentration does not exclude acute hemorrhage before redistribution occurs.

Mixed venous oxygen saturation
Hemorrhage compensation
Right ventricular infarct physiology
questions.why: Inflammatory mediators produce vasodilation, endothelial dysfunction, and altered microcirculatory flow. Early hyperdynamic shock can show low SVR and high CO despite inadequate effective tissue oxygen delivery. Septic shock can later include myocardial depression and low output; the high-output pattern is not universal.
rationales: Inflammatory mediators produce vasodilation, endothelial dysfunction, and altered microcirculatory flow. Early hyperdynamic shock can show low SVR and high CO despite inadequate effective tissue oxygen delivery. In this case: A febrile patient with infection has warm extremities, low systemic resistance, and elevated measured cardiac output.

This option describes mixed venous oxygen saturation: Mixed venous saturation reflects the balance between systemic oxygen delivery and consumption. Low CO often increases extraction and lowers SvO2, whereas sepsis can produce high values when extraction or flow distribution is impaired. The target concept is early septic shock profile. Its defining case is: A febrile patient with infection has warm extremities, low systemic resistance, and elevated measured cardiac output.

This option describes hemorrhage compensation: Arterial baroreflex activation increases sympathetic tone, producing tachycardia, arteriolar constriction, and venoconstriction. RAAS and vasopressin support volume and pressure over longer intervals. The target concept is early septic shock profile. Its defining case is: A febrile patient with infection has warm extremities, low systemic resistance, and elevated measured cardiac output.

This option describes right ventricular infarct physiology: An infarcted RV cannot effectively deliver blood to the left heart, reducing LV preload. Hypotension, elevated JVP, and relatively clear lungs after inferior MI are classic clues. The target concept is early septic shock profile. Its defining case is: A febrile patient with infection has warm extremities, low systemic resistance, and elevated measured cardiac output.

questions.q: After smoke exposure, a patient has headache and tissue hypoxia despite normal arterial oxygen tension and a reassuring conventional pulse oximeter reading. Which concept is best illustrated?
